#2040. Jacob Murphy is not our future but he IS the here and now

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

In the grand and often unforgiving theatre of Premier League football, where stars are minted in bursts of brilliance and extinguished by the next transfer window, there are players whose value is measured not solely in highlight reels but in the quiet accumulation of purpose.

Jacob Murphy belongs to that rarer company.

At 31, the Newcastle United winger continues to embody a particular kind of professional resilience—one forged in loans, tempered by reinvention, and now expressed in moments that still make the away end rise as one.

I know, we’ve heard the complaints of many fans and pundits that Jacob Murphy is “not good enough”, that he disappears for long stretches during the match, that we need an upgrade at the position. Maybe. The lad is not perfect or to everyone’s liking but he is my cup of tea. He produces with first-time crosses into the box, always gives 100%, readily gets back on defence, and adds a bit of needed comic relief.

Born in Wembley on 24 February 1995 to parents with roots in NE England, Murphy carried Newcastle in his blood long before he wore the shirt. A boyhood Magpie who grew up visiting family in Gateshead, he and his twin brother Josh cut their teeth at Norwich City’s academy. Together they helped win the FA Youth Cup in 2013. Jacob’s path thereafter was the classic English apprenticeship of the lower leagues: temporary homes at Swindon, Southend, Blackpool, Scunthorpe, Colchester, and, most formatively, a season-long stay at Coventry City in 2015-16 where he scored ten goals and announced himself as a player of genuine threat. Returning to Norwich, he produced a breakthrough campaign of nearly double figures in goals and assists, enough to persuade Rafa Benítez to bring him to St James’ Park in the summer of 2017 for a fee in the region of £12 million.

The early years on Tyneside were not seamless. There were loans—to West Bromwich Albion and Sheffield Wednesday—and the familiar struggle of a young wide player trying to impose himself in a club that was itself searching for direction (certainly, Steve Bruce was not the man to coach him up).

What changed everything was the arrival of Eddie Howe.

Under Howe, Jacob Murphy was transformed from squad option into indispensable operator. He became the energetic wide presence who pressed, crossed, tracked, and, with increasing frequency, delivered. The 2024-25 season marked his high-water mark: eight Premier League goals and a dozen assists, a body of work that placed him among the league’s most productive creators from the flank. He scored in the Carabao Cup semi-final against Arsenal and provided a decisive assist in the final as Newcastle United ended a 70-year wait for a major domestic trophy. For a player once dismissed by some as a useful squad man, it was validation of the highest order.

Murphy’s assets have never been those of the purest technician or the most glamorous dribbler. He is direct. He is tireless. He possesses a left foot capable of bending a ball from distance with sudden, almost unfair venom, and a right foot that can pick out a player in the box. Was Alexander Isak worth the money Liverpool paid without the assists of Murphy? I’d argue that we got top money from the Reds for the rat – and Murphy’s crosses were a major contributor. His willingness to occupy the spaces that make others look better. He crosses with purpose, contributes defensively without complaint, and brings a structural intelligence that managers prize.

In a squad that has undergone significant change—younger faces arriving, senior voices departing—his experience has become a form of quiet leadership. Even after being omitted from the formal player leadership group under new head coach Matthias Jaissle, Murphy has spoken of an unchanged responsibility: to add value, to set standards, to help the younger players understand what the Premier League demands week after week.

This season has been more measured than the explosion of 2024-25. Minutes have been shared; the goal tally has been slower to climb. Yet the importance remains as he’s more dependable than Anthony Elanga and much more experienced that Matias Fernandez-Pardo.

On a November afternoon at Craven Cottage, with Newcastle searching for a response after consecutive defeats, Murphy produced the kind of moment that defines him. Intercepting a loose pass, he drove forward, cut inside, and from fully 25 yards unleashed a curling left-footed strike that left Bernd Leno helpless. The goal was his first of the campaign. It was also a reminder.

Three minutes later Fulham equalised (of course they did) but the point was earned in part because of that individual quality and the industry that preceded it. Days earlier he had provided an assist in a clean-sheet victory at Crystal Palace. The pattern is familiar: when Newcastle need a spark or a measure of control on the flank, Murphy is often the player trusted to provide it.

There is something almost old-fashioned in his story. In an era of astronomical fees and instantaneous celebrity, Murphy has built a career through persistence, adaptation, and an unshowy professionalism. He has scored against Manchester City in his early days, netted a brace against Tottenham (including a scorcher!), contributed to European nights and a first major trophy in generations. He has survived the doubts that accompany any player who does not fit the neatest marketing narrative. Now, with his contract situation under discussion and interest from elsewhere already rejected by the club, he continues to state the obvious with clarity: he knows what he brings.

I am not advocating that Jacob Murphy is our future but he IS the here and now. The best we have at his position and, until we can get in a player with better talent and upside, indispensable for the team this season.

For Newcastle United in this transitional season under Jaissle, that contribution—energy, experience, the capacity for the sudden decisive strike—remains quietly essential. Jacob Murphy does not demand the spotlight. He simply continues to occupy the spaces where the game is still won, one determined run, one precise cross, one unforgettable curler at a time.

In the long narrative of a club that has known both glory and patience, his is a chapter written in steady ink. I think its time to give him some respect. 🎙️ THE MAG PODCAST Ep 15: Fulham frustration, Newcastle United’s season report card and Relegation fears Listen to the latest episode of The Mag Pod! #2038. Arsenal Women held by London City Lionesses despite Frida Maanum goal

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal Women missed the chance to end their frustrating run of draws at home as London City Lionesses came from behind to earn a 1-1 draw at the Emirates Stadium.

Frida Maanum gave the Gunners the lead in an exciting start to the game. But Isobel Goodwin equalised almost straight away. Despite creating plenty of chances, Renée Slegers’ side failed to find a second goal.

Arsenal have now lost their last five WSL games at the Emirates. The results were yet another frustrating afternoon for the defending champions, who put in a strong display against Barcelona in Europe earlier in the week.

Arsenal started on a high note, creating some dangerous chances with their quick play. Emily Fox and Lisa Baum worked really well together down the right, and Ona Batlle had a great chance from the edge of the box.

As the pressure mounted, Fox surged forward and played a perfectly weighted through ball to Alessia Russo. The striker turned and played the ball back to Maanum, who rounded off her impressive comeback from injury by finishing.

Arsenal had little time to rejoice. London City equalised just a minute later as Goodwin found herself in space to fire past Misa Rodríguez.

The visitors looked more confident after equalising, but Mary Earps was proving a tough ask for Arsenal to score past. The ex-Manchester United shot-stopper kept out Baum and made some key stops from Arsenal’s efforts.

Rodriguez also had to make a key stop before half-time as she got a hand to Daniela Arques Lazaro’s powerful strike to keep the scores level.

The Gunners continued their attacking play but were made to work hard by a high pressing side from London City.

But Arsenal still managed to create some chances. Caitlin Foord put Earps under pressure and Maanum and Baum combined before the latter saw her curl just wide.

London City posed a threat too. With Kadidiatou Diani and Grace Geyoro causing defensive problems for Arsenal, Geyoro fired into the side netting.

Delphine Cascarino had the game’s defining moment of the second half, hitting the crossbar from outside the box. However, Arsenal were lucky to escape and Maanum came close to winning the game, hitting the woodwork from a dangerous counter.

Slegers brought on Kyra Cooney-Cross and Olivia Smith in the 72nd minute to provide some new energy. Smith looked lively upon entering the game, but Earps denied her efforts and Batlle’s cross.

Emily Fox had to be substituted due to injury in the final moments of the game, but Slegers later indicated that she would be okay.

The Gunners were unable to find a winning goal and will now turn their attention to their Champions League clash on Thursday with Lyon. They will then face West Ham at home in the WSL.

#2037. 9 rule changes to help the referee cut out cheating and make the game fairer

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

The referee and his role in what’s wrong with football.

One of the many problems with football in England is the refereeing.

Not necessarily the refs themselves, more the ever-changing guidance and policies they are expected to obey when it comes to their refereeing.

The Premier League is the world’s most popular, watched all around the globe on television in far higher numbers than any other rival.

It is a money-spinning product that cannot afford to lose its pre-eminent position. Those in charge, such as Richard Masters, the Premier League’s chief executive, have millions of reasons to protect the brand.

In his particular case, 2.6 million for the financial year ending on July 31, 2025. That included a £1.1m bonus awarded in part for his help in negotiating record-breaking broadcasting deals with Sky, TNT and Amazon.

That £2.6m remuneration package (as they like to say in the City of London) was £700,000 up on the previous year. Don’t expect any reduction when the 2025-26 figures are lodged at Companies House . . .

The Premier League’s popularity relies on more than having some of the world’s best players. It also depends on the characteristic style of play being distinctly different from La Liga or the Bundesliga or Serie A. Which is where the refereeing comes in.

You might believe a referee’s primary role is to ensure, to the best of his ability, the game is played fairly. You might be right, though I suspect the job of protecting the brand has become the driving force for the man in the middle and his colleagues.

The more free kicks, the less attractive the spectacle. Those in charge of the Premier League cannot afford a stop-start product, because viewer figures are paramount.

Pro Ref knows this, the players know this, the managers know this. That’s why so many fouls go unpunished. Not because the referees should go to Specsavers. They see them and choose to ignore them.

It’s the coward’s way. Or should that be Howard’s Way? Mr Webb, the head of Pro Ref, was pilloried when VAR kept halting the action. He responded by telling the boys and girls at Stockley Park to intervene in only the most extreme cases.

Outcome: a non-decision by the ref is not corrected by the VAR.

The most blatant mistakes are later scrutinised by the Premier League’s key match incidents panel. Its verdicts read like an Orwellian nightmare.

In a typical case, a penalty is not awarded for foul play. The VAR, obeying Howard’s Way, looks and agrees. Days later, the key match incidents panel says: “A penalty was probably the right call but VAR was correct in doing nothing. If the ref had blown for the foul, the VAR would have agreed.”

So there you have it. Whichever call the referee makes is correct. It must be, because the VAR backed him up. Reminds me of the olden days when the referee’s decision was final.

Before each season starts, changes are announced to the way the laws of the game will be enforced. Among recent initiatives was the five-second countdown on throws and goal kicks if the referee detected time wasting. They are rarely enforced because the threat of being penalised has encouraged quicker play, as intended. There’s also a 10-second limit for a substituted player to leave the field.

Nobody would argue against those changes, though they smack of window dressing when much more important problems are being ignored. Here are just a few suggestions to make the game fairer.

1. Warn any player who refuses to retreat 10 yards promptly from an opponent’s free kick. The second time he or a teammate does it, book the offender. Third time, red card.

2. Issue a yellow card for pushing whenever no attempt is made to play the ball.

3. Award a throw-in to the other team if the ball is not released from behind the head. Or if both feet are not grounded behind the touchline. Or if the throw is taken more than two yards forward of the right point. Players know.

4) Book any player who pulls an opponent’s shirt, shorts or socks.

5) Stop players taking free kicks from the wrong spot. If they do it again, book them. Keepers in particular move the ball up the field or towards their goal with impunity, knowing the referee will do nothing.

6) A yellow card for all offences of dissent, either physical or verbal, directed at the referee or his assistants. Including the captain.

7) An automatic card to any player who dives. In the opponents’ penalty area, make it a red.

8) Add on at least one minute for every goal celebration.

9) Play an advantage if there is the chance of one but go back and book any player who has fouled off the ball.

You might think there would be a blizzard of yellow and red cards. I believe the far more likely consequence would be a massive reduction in gamesmanship, cheating, time wasting and other examples of the dark arts that are blighting the beautiful game.

Once players realised they couldn’t foul with impunity, they would quickly learn to play the game as a sport, rather than as a cynical win-at-all-costs exercise.

#2036. Declan Rice’s latest Arsenal evolution shows why Arteta wanted him tied down

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Declan Rice’s new contract shows how much of an asset he is to Mikel Arteta. His recent performances show why.

The England international has reportedly signed a new five-year deal which will keep him at the Emirates Stadium until 2031. The contract is a reward for the midfielder who has been instrumental in Arsenal’s success since he moved to the club in 2023 from West Ham.

Rice has not just provided the presence and protection that Arsenal were hoping for with their £105 million signing. He has continued to develop his game, especially after returning to his deeper midfield role this season.

Rice came in as a defensive midfielder, but Arteta quickly saw how much he could offer higher up the park.

His physicality, ability to run into the box and set piece threat made him a useful left-sided number eight. Rice had a huge impact in midfield for Arsenal, bringing goals and a new attacking threat.

But Rice has played in a more advanced position on the right-hand side of the midfield duo this season, and this has not limited his impact but instead highlighted another key part of his game.

Rice has made the most line-breaking passes in the Premier League this season, with Opta stats reported by Sky Sports showing he is second only to Premier League players.

This is of particular interest, as he has often come under criticism for his distribution. But he is averaging nearly double the amount of line-breaking passes he did last season.

While his running ability is still an asset, he is also becoming much better at penetrating through the defensive lines to find his teammates, giving Arsenal another option to move the ball forward with.

The development of Rice is key in securing a new contract at Arsenal.

The 27-year-old has already proven to be one of the most reliable members of Arteta’s squad and has shown great longevity by only missing five games out of his 119 Premier League outings in his first spell at the club.

Former West Ham teammate Jack Wilshere has also praised Rice’s strong work ethic, ability to adapt and natural leadership qualities.

The reported 5-year deal will keep Rice at Arsenal until 2031, into his early 30s. While the terms of the deal have yet to be signed, it is a huge statement from the club.

They are not only rewarding Rice for what he has done but also investing in what he can do.

With Arteta finding new ways to utilise Rice’s qualities in midfield, Rice could still have some of his best years ahead of him.

#2035. West Ham Fans Asked to Unite in Memory of 19-Year-Old Supporter Luke

The loss of a young person reverberates far beyond their immediate family. Today, we are sharing Luke’s story in the hope of raising awareness, encouraging compassion, and supporting a tribute that means so much to those left behind.

Remembering Luke: A Young Life Gone Too Soon

At just 19 years old, Luke’s life was tragically cut short, leaving a family, circle of friends, and wider community struggling to come to terms with an unimaginable loss.

Known affectionately as “Lukey” and “Little Man” by those closest to him, Luke was a devoted West Ham United supporter and a loyal season ticket holder.

As they continue to navigate their grief, Luke’s family have made a simple but heartfelt request.

They are asking West Ham supporters attending the upcoming home fixture against Preston to join together in a minute of applause during the 19th minute of the match, marking the age at which Luke passed away.

The tribute is intended as a celebration of his life and a visible reminder that no family should feel alone during their darkest moments.

A shirt bearing Luke’s name will be placed on his seat in the stadium, providing a poignant symbol of the empty space left by his passing.

By sharing Luke’s story, we hope not only to support his family but also to encourage conversations around loss, grief, and the importance of supporting one another through difficult times.

C&H encourage anyone attending the match, or anyone who sees Luke’s story online, to help spread the word and support the planned tribute.

On the 19th minute, every clap will be a reminder that Luke’s life touched many people and that his memory continues to live on through his family, friends, and fellow supporters.

Our thoughts are with everyone who knew and loved Luke.

If this story resonates with you, please share it to help ensure Luke receives the tribute his family and friends are hoping for. Sometimes the smallest act of support can make the biggest difference.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

#2034. The Mike Ashley relegations pre Newcastle United takeover and lessons to be learnt

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

I hold my hands up that I was guilty of a bit of an oversight during The Mag Podcast last week.

“Those who do not learn from the past are doomed to repeat it” – George Santayana

I half remembered the quote above and threw it to my co-host Hutch on The Mag Pod to try and recite it verbatim, as he likes history and stuff like that.

There were two errors involved to be fair, me for putting him on the spot like that, and Hutch for being as thick as mince.

Jamie puts Hutch on the spot over Newcastle United’s relegation history

Anyway, I’ve since found the appropriate wording and replicated as a starting point here, as a way of conveying what we’ve been doing on The Mag Pod as we tried to fill the ongoing international break. Basically, there has been some chatter and paranoia that the issues this Newcastle United side are facing this season could well lead to a relegation battle. If it does turn out that way, it won’t be any of our first rodeos.

However, it’s fair to say that many of those Mike Ashley era struggles ended fairly benignly, with the drop avoided. On occasions this was comfortably, at times it was squeaky, but it didn’t really matter as long as you lived to fight another day. Unfortunately, there were exceptions.

So, to try and learn the lessons of history, we have used this round of podcasts to look at the Mike Ashley seasons where it went terribly wrong.

Late last week the first instalment (Episode 16) dropped, as we took a walk through the chaotic 2008-09 season. The follow-up, reliving the relegation of 2015-16 (Episode 17), which is out now.

These serve as both a wander through times gone by and a study in what we can learn.

Ideally, listeners may feel better about current circumstances in comparison with the poor decisions, awful form and careless business that led to highly avoidable seasons away from the Premier League under the previous regime.

Unfortunately there may be times when certain things ring true and we appear in real danger of breaking Mr Santayana’s above rule.

There is a third instalment to come as well, but alas we are a bit wet behind the lugs to fully recount the demotion of 1988-89.

Instead, a slight change of tack is incoming where Thursday’s edition (Episode 18) will see a review of the 2020-21 season, the final year before the Newcastle United takeover. This is to give a perspective on how far we have come, the impact of the considerable changes since and to hopefully make you all feel better you’re no longer looking at Steve Bruce.

Spoiler alert, but the general overall conclusion of these editions is that more time and consideration is needed in the current circumstances, to really have a full and proper idea of how badly it may compare to some of our darker times. However, there are things in there that may very well resonate.

Please enjoy The Mag Podcast and we’d love your feedback on what we have done so far and suggestions for the future in the commenting section below.

#2033. Martin Zubimendi sends fresh Arsenal message as January transfer speculation grows

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Martin Zubimendi has raised questions among Arsenal fans over his future. This follows comments from the midfielder that he is keen to succeed in north London despite struggling for game time this season.

The Spain international has been linked with a move to Chelsea, Atletico Madrid and Real Madrid ahead of the January transfer window. Reports from Spain have said that Zubimendi’s situation at the club is becoming more complex, with the player possibly being available.

Zubimendi has also spoken about the speculation. In his interview during the international break with Marca, he said he did not feel like he was near to a move to Atletico, and he is still delighted to be in London.

He added the 27-year-old has had no contact with any other clubs. His priority is to get into Arteta’s squad.

This is an interesting response to the transfer speculation that has been building. Arsenal may well attract interest for one of their midfielders. However, there does not appear to be any evidence that Zubimendi is actively looking to leave.

In his first season, he played 38 times in the Premier League and became an important member of Arteta’s midfield. However, he has not started a league game this season.

Opta Analyst shows that he has only played 100 minutes in the Premier League in seven games. He has also faced increased competition for a spot in the team with the arrival of Bruno Guimarães.

Myles Lewis-Skelly is also an option in the middle of the park. Zubimendi will have to fight for his place back.

It is understood Arteta had a chat with Zubimendi ahead of the campaign and made it clear he would face more competition from the new signings and would have to earn his place.

Zubimendi has accepted the challenge and has said he could see it as a chance to learn and improve due to his reduced workload.

The interest from Spain and Chelsea will make it a tough choice if the right offers come in. However, losing Zubimendi will mean Arteta won’t have as many options to call upon in the busy second half of the season.

But he proved his worth in the game against Slavia Prague earlier this month. He started the Champions League match and played the full 90 minutes.

This shows that his contribution shouldn’t be judged purely on how much he plays in the Premier League. Arsenal will have a busy schedule in Europe and domestically, and he may provide some much-needed quality in the midfield.

With Zubimendi contracted until 2030, there is no immediate reason for Arsenal to look to sell him. He will have time to fight for his spot in the starting XI.

Despite not making a commitment to remain at the club beyond January, his remarks indicate that he is not on the lookout for alternatives.

The priority for Arsenal will be trying to find a way to get the best out of Zubimendi. He was a regular last season and seems happy to wait for his chance.

This company will ‘consolidate RedBird’s Milan-based investments in sports, infrastructure, and entertainment’ and organise individual assets into a ‘multi-sport platform’.

The report continues, stating that MSE will help to further transform Milano into one of the ‘most influential sports and entertainment markets in the world’ by combining its importance in fashion, design, culture, sports and entertainment.

Above all, though, it’s another representation of RedBird’s long-term investment and commitment to the club (and the city).

Finally, RedBird have formed a new leadership team for the group, with Brett Yormark appointed the CEO of the company. He will report directly to Cardinale and will lead the ‘development and implementation of MSE’s strategy, overseeing current portfolio businesses and evaluating future investment opportunities.’

#2031. Viktor Gyökeres’ Sweden resurgence raises Arsenal questions, but the January exit is far from certain

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Viktor Gyökeres is reminding Arsenal of his prolific goal scoring capabilities.

The striker found the back of the net twice in Sweden’s 3-2 Nations League win against Bosnia and Herzegovina on November 14, both times from the spot to take his total to four in the Nations League this season.

The win also means they have booked their place in League A with one match left to play in the group, and Gyökeres has certainly played his part in this excellent run.

However, the performance will raise questions about his future at the club. The idea that he may be leaving in January is a possibility that needs to be looked at.

There is a stark difference between his international and club form.

Gyökeres has only played 181 minutes in seven Premier League games this season, starting just once as Kai Havertz has usually been preferred in central areas.

However, he has had more opportunities to play in European competition. Gyökeres has started three of Arsenal’s four matches in the Champions League, scoring one goal and providing two assists.

Gyökeres is not totally out of Arteta’s plans, but he will not play much domestically.

He has been in fine form internationally recently. Sweden are building their attack around his movement and penalty area presence, meaning he will have chances to regularly perform.

However, just because he is doing well internationally does not mean he will start regularly for the club. Arteta has other attacking options and tactics to consider.

There have been suggestions surrounding Gyökeres’ future, with reports that Arsenal may look to add more attacking flair to their squad.

AC Milan and Juventus have also been linked, but there is no agreement or suggestion that either club is looking to make a January move for the forward.

Gyökeres has opened up about the speculation.

In an interview with Swedish media outlet Fotbollskanalen during the international break, he stated that he would like to stay at the club. The player also denied any issues with his relationship with Arteta, stating that they have good communication.

However, the player may not stay forever, as he has not played much in the Premier League so far. If this continues, and Arsenal sign another forward, it could cause an issue.

For now, though, there is little evidence that Gyökeres is trying to leave the club.

He’ll be looking to get regular game time at 28 after finding his scoring touch with Sweden. Arsenal will also need to work out how to use him best as a goalscoring striker.

But for now the January speculation seems a little early. He has stated he wants to stay at Arsenal, and the next few weeks may prove to be more important.

Facing a late fitness test, it seems Solomon is putting caution to one side in his desperation to be part of the Israel national team to take on Austria tomorrow.

#2029. Now entering the debate on whether Bruno Guimaraes is returning Toon hero or Toon turncoat

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

I have been reading lately, with interest, the conversations surrounding the return of Bruno Guimaraes to St James’ Park this coming weekend (Saturday 21st November)

Opinion seems to be split as to what kind of reception our former captain should receive if he is selected to face us on Saturday evening.

Since leaving Newcastle United, Bruno Guimaraes hasn’t been an automatic starter, so we may not have the chance to show him our collective feelings either way.

From what I am reading the camp seems to be split directly down the middle between “Bruno Guimaraes is a hero who led us to our first silverware in decades”, to “Bruno Guimaraes is a traitor who went all out to manufacture a move away from the club.”

Looking back now at the summer dealings it’s easier to reflect on what happened and why the players who left, did.

In my opinion , it was only a matter of time before Sandro left us, his heart never seemed in the Northeast, neither does it in North London to be honest, the only time I think we will see him truly happy is when he is plying his trade back in Italy, unfortunately for him it doesn’t look as if Italian football could subsidise that kind of financial arrangement.

Again, in my opinion the same can be said about Anthony Gordon, I liked the lad but also got the impression he thought he was destined for a bigger club, something which was proven to be true.

I just got the impression he thought he was too big a name for the club and it was a matter of time before he left. The fact he went abroad seemed to make the move slightly more palatable as a Newcastle fan.

And on to Bruno, I love(d) the bloke, I was stood in the away section of the Stadium of light, with 7,000 others, 3-0 up and watched him slide tackle on our own goal line and celebrate as if he had scored.

I loved his passion and enthusiasm for the game and the Toon. He could drive and win a game single handedly by grabbing the team by the scruff of the neck and pushing the team forward.

I loved his speech at the Town Moor presentation and the way he appreciated the character of the Northeast.

Will I boo him if he plays on Saturday? 100%. This is not out of spite; I take this decision more so on a few factors.

Bruno Guimaraes is a confidence player; we have seen this ourselves over the years. We know he feels bad about leaving, he has made a few statements leading up to the game about the toughest decision he has had to make-blah blah blah etc.

But, he went out of his way to hire a super-agent in Kia Joorabchian to help get a move away. Not the actions of a player in love with the glorious Northeast.

He had opportunities to soften the blow of leaving many times over the course of the 2026 World Cup but chose the coward’s way out with total silence, despite the obvious effect it would have on the fans

Let’s get at him, rattle him, affect his confidence, and take the roof off every time Dan Burn cuts him in half, maybe that will be enough to unsettle him and his teammates.

Newcastle United are in a transitional period as a team, but I still feel on a Saturday evening kick off, with a crowd fuelled with day drinking we can beat anyone..

Maybe spare applause for Bruno Guimaraes at the end for his service to the club, I will.

#2028. David Raya and Jurrien Timber deals show Arsenal are serious about protecting their title-winning core

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal are continuing their excellent work in retaining their key players as David Raya and Jurrien Timber have both been approached about new contracts.

This comes after Declan Rice signed a five-year contract extension. The midfielder will now stay at the Emirates until 2031, but Mikel Arteta is now close to locking down more defenders in his squad.

Timber has reportedly agreed better terms, and Raya is also on the verge of a new deal. Although both deals are yet to be officially announced, it shows how important Arsenal are trying to keep them at the top.

The importance of retaining Raya and Timber is evident.

Since arriving at the club from Brentford, Raya has become Arteta’s first choice in goal. He has become an important part of Arsenal’s attacking play due to his distribution, decision-making and game under pressure.

His performances have also earned him honours outside of North London as he was named in the 2026 FIFPRO World 11. Only the second Arsenal player to win the award after Thierry Henry in 2006.

Raya has a contract in place until 2028, although he was given better financial terms last year. However, a new long-term deal will offer more security to one of Arteta’s most trusted players.

Since joining from Ajax in 2023, Timber has become a key part of Arsenal’s backline. Despite injury issues, he has proven to be one of the most dependable defenders in the squad.

He can play as a right back, left back and centre back which provides Arteta with great versatility. He has the physicality and technical ability to help Arsenal at both ends of the pitch.

It has been reported that Timber has agreed to better terms. How long his contract is for is unknown.

There is a pattern beginning to emerge from Arsenal’s recent contract news.

Rice has been signed until 2031. Timber is also expected to sign, committing his peak years to the club. Raya is also expected to sign soon, with talks said to be at an advanced stage.

Arteta recently signed a contract extension until 2030. They aren’t just trying to keep their best players for another year but are looking to create consistency within the squad and management.

This is an issue for any club competing within the domestic and European leagues, as it can cause problems with team cohesion and development due to constant change of key players.

While there is still work to be done, this is positive news for fans.

Signing Raya and Timber will ensure that two key components of Arteta’s backline are safe. It will also show that with Rice’s new contract, they’re looking to build on their recent success and not let their best players near the end of their contracts.

#2027. Arsenal’s Piero Hincapié contract plans show how quickly his importance has grown

Lucie Turner writes about Arsenal for Read Arsenal and Newcastle United for Read Newcastle. A long-time Arsenal supporter, she also follows rugby, snooker, darts and Formula 1. Her work covers match previews and reports, breaking news, player profiles and opinion pieces.

Arsenal are said to be trying to reward Piero Hincapié with better contract terms after just months since making his move permanent.

According to reports, negotiations are at an advanced stage between the Ecuadorian and international players. David Raya is also near to signing a new contract as Mikel Arteta looks to retain his key squad members.

However, Hincapié is in a slightly different position compared to his teammates. The 24-year-old only signed a five-year deal permanently in the summer.

Therefore, he could be discussing an increase in his salary rather than an extension. It has not been officially confirmed by either Arsenal or the player.

Arsenal have exercised their option to make Hincapié’s loan move from Bayer Leverkusen permanent.

The defender made 39 appearances in all competitions during his first season in North London, scoring one goal and providing two assists. He has become an important part of Arteta’s defensive options.

His versatility has been an asset to Arsenal. His ability to play as a centre-back or left-back meaning he provides another option to utilise when problems occur with injuries or rotation in defence.

However, Hincapié has been overshadowed by Gabriel Magalhães and Riccardo Calafiori, making it a tough battle for playing time.

In the current campaign, he has played just five games in the league, with all of them coming off the bench. A total of 67 minutes has been played.

Hincapié will not be too concerned by this, as Arsenal have plenty of defensive options, and he provides cover in two positions.

The news that Hincapié is in talks is part of a bigger story around the club trying to keep their best players.

Declan Rice has signed a new five-year deal with Jurrien Timber, signing on improved terms. Raya is also said to be close to signing a new deal.

Arteta has already signed his future to the club until 2030. It is clear that they want to keep the continuity going forward after recent success.

While Hincapié has a contract until next year, renegotiating his deal would show how much Arsenal values him.

They may want to reward their players who have quickly become key members of their squad.

He has no reports of being unhappy and looking to leave the club. It seems he is being rewarded for his contributions to the club and to give him security in the long term.

This is a huge vote of confidence for a player who has only just completed his permanent move this summer.

#2026. Lewis Hall desperate to leave Newcastle United and join Manchester United relegation scrap…really?

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Lewis Hall is the best English left-back by a country mile, Lewis Hall is the best left-back in the Premier League, Lewis Hall is going to join Manchester United in January 2027.

As we were reminded in this past week of internationals, Lewis Hall is indeed the Premier League’s and England’s best left-back.

The lifelong Newcastle United fan was the best player on the pitch when England defeated Croatia at Wembley on Thursday.

Then on Sunday he was up there as once again one of England’s very best players as they won 3-2 against World Cup holders Spain, with Lewis Hall outclassing their most dangerous player, Lamine Yamal.

So of course the natural outcome is that Lewis Hall will now sign for Manchester United in January…

Twenty years ago, Manchester United had won eight Premier League titles in the previous 14 seasons and never finished lower than third across that time period.

Back in November 2006, Manchester United were well on their way to reclaiming the Premier League title, they would win three in a row and five in seven, finishing runners-up in the other two.

From the 1991-92 season to the 2012-13 season, those 22 seasons saw Manchester United win 13 titles, six times runners-up, three times finishing third.

These last 13 seasons Manchester United have not won a single Premier League title, eight of the 13 they have finished outside the top three.

The last three Premier League seasons Manchester United have included a 15th place and an 8th place one and are currently sitting in the relegation zone after only one Premier League win in the last six months.

So of course Lewis Hall is desperate to join Manchester United…

The lifelong Newcastle United fan was eight years old when Man U last lifted the Premier League title.

Exactly why thirteen and a half years later would the best left-back in the Premier League would have even minimal interest  in signing for Manchester United?

Yet this is what the Manchester United fans, the Manchester United loving media, as well as other desperate idiots, want us all to believe.

Funnily enough, none of them give any reasons as to why this should be the case.

Nothing logical anyway, nothing that makes sense.

The best they would come out with is something along the lines of…”Well, it is Manchester United.”

Which ironically hits the nail squarely on the head, it is Manchester United.

It isn’t one of the successful clubs, it is one that used to be successful many years ago, during the first eight years Lewis Hall was on this earth, not the near decade and a half that has followed.

Lewis Hall now has the world at his feet and will have choices to make.

Will he stay forever at the club he and his family have supported all of their lives, or will he at some point join a club that appears to have a lot more chance of winning trophies?

Neither of those options feature Manchester United.

Yet I have seen so many journalists and pundits yet again embarrass themselves, after his stellar performances for England, talk about Lewis Hall set to move to Manchester United. Rather than talk about just how good he is for Newcastle United and vital to this current season (and hopefully beyond).

As an extra amusing aside, we also have the following…

On 29 May 2023 it was announced that Mauricio Pochettino would be appointed as head coach of Chelsea on 1 July 2023, on a two-year contract with an option to extend for another year.

On 22 August 2023, Lewis Hall joined Newcastle United on a season-long loan with an obligation to buy for £28 million, plus £7 million in add-ons (On 1 November, he scored his first goal for Newcastle United in a 3-0 League Cup win against Manchester United at Old Trafford. Then on 15 May 2024, Lewis Hall scored his first ever Premier League goal for United against Man U at Old Trafford…).

Amusingly, the new Manchester United boss Mauricio Pochettino was the Chelsea boss who sold Lewis Hall to Newcastle United. Pochettino selling Hall without even first playing him in a competitive match.

Of course, the reality is that at basket cases clubs Chelsea and Manchester United, the manager/head coach has no say in which players are bought or sold. So Mauricio Pochettino had no say on whether Chelsea sold Lewis Hall back in August 2023, just the same as Mauricio Pochettino will have no say in January 2027 if Manchester United embarrass themselves with an approach to try and ‘tempt’ (and fail, obviously) Lewis Hall to join Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s Old Trafford circus.

#2024. I won't do a Mauricio Pochettino! Thomas Tuchel insists there is 'zero chance' he will walk out on England for a Premier League job - but admits he misses club football

Published: 14:00 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 15:19 EST, 11 November 2026

Thomas Tuchel will stay loyal to England until the end of his contract at the 2028 European Championship but admits that he does miss the regular thrill of club management.

As Mauricio Pochettino prepares to activate a release clause with the USA national team to take the Manchester United job, England boss Tuchel has vowed to ignore all outside offers until the end of his deal with England.

‘There is no release clause,’ said Tuchel. ‘I signed the contract. I want to stay until the Euros. I want to do the Euros. We have unfinished business.’

After that Tuchel said that he is open-minded.

Asked whether he could stay longer with England, he said with a smile that: ‘I am open to everything.’

The chances are, though, that England will be looking for a new coach once the 2028 Euros are done.

Thomas Tuchel has revealed he misses club football - but won't walk out on England

He enjoys the buzz of managing 50 matches per season but is contracted until 2028

‘I miss the 50 [club] matches a season,’ Tuchel said. ‘I miss those two minutes when everything is done. You go out the two minutes before the first whistle goes. It's like the best two minutes.

‘Everything is done. You're in a full stadium. Lights are on and you're just so excited and you're part of it.

‘That's actually the two minutes where I realise how lucky and how grateful I am. Then the whistle goes, and then you're just in the tunnel again, trying to win the game for your team.’

Tuchel originally signed a short-term deal through to last summer’s World Cup but extended it until the Euros in the months before the tournament that ended with a semi-final defeat to Argentina.

Asked if there was ‘zero chance’ of him leaving before the end of his contract, he said: ‘I would say so.

‘First of all, I'm very grateful for what I have here because I know how rare it is to be in love with your team and to have the trust and to be able to work freely with your coaching staff, which I am.

‘I love my group of players. I love my staff and I have bosses who trust me and are happy with the way we do things.

Pochettino is set to become the new manager of Manchester United, replacing Michael Carrick

‘So, it's a lot. And I know how to appreciate it a lot.

‘It's in a good place. I'm in a good place. I'm desperate to win the Nations League and to play and try to win the Euros.’

England face Croatia at Wembley tonight in the Nations League before heading to Madrid for their final group game against Spain on Sunday. If England win both matches, they will top their group ahead of next March’s quarter-finals. At the very least they should progress as a second placed team.

The four teams emerging from next spring’s quarters will play Nations League semi-finals and final in one country next summer. With a venue yet to be chosen by UEFA, the FA are expected to throw their hat into the ring as a prospective host.

Tuchel has spoken before about the struggles England sometimes have in taking training performances on to the pitch and agreed that hosting the Nations League latter stages could act as a decent warm up before the challenges of playing a big tournament in front of a home crowd a year later.

‘The Nations League helps in general for us and I think to have it here could be exciting,’ Tuchel said.

‘It would be nice to have it here. So first of all, we need to reach the final before we play.

‘Playing at home is a challenge. It should be a home advantage when we go to the Euros and it should not become a home disadvantage that we feel in our brain.

‘It should be exciting and that's why it's also important what we are building at the moment and how the team plays.’

#2023. Cardinale discusses MSE creation and evolution within Milan: “Helping write a new chapter”

With the news of the new company leading AC Milan, Gerry Cardinale has offered a few words about what it means for the project.

In recent minutes, RedBird have announced a new parent company for Milan, aptly named ‘Milan Sports & Entertainment’. It’s a project that aims to put all of the club’s investments under one umbrella, whilst also allowing further investment into the city.

The new stadium is believed to have played a big part in this decision, and the Rossoneri will hopefully benefit significantly from this move.

As MilanNews relays, Cardinale offered some words in the announcement about the creation of the company, what it means to the city and for Rossoneri fans, what it means for the club.

“Over the past 25 years, we have worked alongside rights holders in the sports and media sectors to create innovative businesses that have transformed their respective industries.

“This evolution is based on a deep respect for the intellectual property assets that underpin these businesses, a long-term partnership with rights holders, and the ambition to fully unlock the potential of these teams and leagues, both on and off the pitch.

“Milan Sports & Entertainment represents the culmination of this journey and the work we have carried out since we first invested in AC Milan four years ago. Becoming a club owner has given us an even deeper understanding of what creates long-term value: winning, serving fans, and investing in the communities that give these institutions meaning.

“Today, we apply this experience on a different scale: not just to a single club, a single sport, or a single facility, but to an entire city and a portfolio that spans sports, lifestyle, and entertainment. I have known Brett Yormark and worked with him for 25 years.

“We’ve been working with Milan for years, and I can’t imagine a better executive in the international sports industry to help execute this strategy. Thanks to Brett, we can bring the best of American sports and live entertainment to Milan, helping write a new chapter in the city’s growth and international success.

“With AC Milan as our cornerstone, which will always be the driving force behind all our initiatives, we intend to build a world-class sports and entertainment platform capable of shaping the future of Milan and European sports, and bringing it back to the forefront of the global stage.”

Considering how much attention Cardinale has paid to the future of the Diavolo, and taking them back to the top level, it’s nice to hear it referenced once again in his latest statement. Hopefully this move is another step towards that.

#2021. Writing’s on the wall for West Ham stalwart’s international career

Time catches up with all of us, footballers just the same. Few are given much indication that the writing is on the wall, until suddenly that place which was automatically theirs is going to a younger, fitter, faster team mate – and then, suddenly, without a fanfare, almost always without even a ‘thank you’ –  it is over.

That, sadly, is likely to be the outcome for Czech stalwart and former captain Tomas Soucek who found himself an unused substitute last night after appearing for just five minutes in his countries’ previous game – during which Tornado Tom’s mistake in added time gifted Spain the injury time second goal in their 2 – 0 defeat of the Czechs.

A total of 93 appearances – 42 as captain – and nineteen goals is a pretty stellar international career and for Soucek to have fought his way back from such a bad injury at the World Cup last summer shows his fighting spirit.

You’d think it unlikely that Soucek will make the squad in the March window, after being virtually discarded for the two Nations League games just gone – both of which his Czech Republic side lost.

Hopefully it’ll give the veteran a little more gusto to complete the job and see his West Ham side over the line and promoted back to the Premier League – which would be a fitting swan song for Soucek who’d be 32 next season and probably a bit-part player if the Hammers make it back to the top tier.

At least it’d mean domestically, he could go out at the top. Which he thoroughly deserves after more than 250 West Ham caps.

#2018. HARRY KANE INTERVIEW: England captain opens up on having an 'ego', the secret behind Ballon d'Or glory, the 'tough' moments with his country - and why he isn't finished yet

Published: 14:00 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 16:11 EST, 11 November 2026

Harry Kane is contemplating his ego. England’s humble superstar, believes the outside world at least, does not have one. He laughs when reminded of his endearing habit of fiddling with his suit buttons during his Ballon d’Or acceptance speech.

But there must, surely, be one example beneath the modest exterior when he descends into a diva?

‘That's a great question. I’m sure my wife will be able to say a thing or two!’ he returns. ‘But ego is funny, because ego is many different things. I guess I have an ego to be the best, because I want to be the best. I just don't do it in a show-off way.’

Kane does have an ego, only it is measured in goals and self-improvement, not vanity and self-indulgence. He has the records because he wants the records, and he wants them more than all of his rivals. He played more games and scored more goals than Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal last season. After his 126th cap against Croatia tonight, he would have played more games and scored more goals than any player in England’s history. He wants those records to stand, too. Ego, you see.

‘Jude (Bellingham) and Declan (Rice), they're on 60-odd caps already and you look at how young they are,’ says Kane, as we chat at England’s base at the Tottenham Hotspur training ground. ‘So I'll try and give them a good number to catch! The goal record (currently 91) is going to be the one that's difficult to beat. I think that’s good!’

It’s better than good, Harry. It is hard to believe now, but Kane was billed as a one-season wonder after his 31-goal breakthrough campaign at Tottenham 11 years ago. He remembers that, just like he does rejection by Arsenal aged eight years old, his missed penalty against France at World Cup 2022, the loan spell at Norwich when he was demoted to the reserves and the loan at Leicester when he sat alone in his flat and wondered if he was good enough for the Premier League.

England captain Harry Kane has admitted he has 'an ego to be the best' after winning the Ballon d'Or

‘I’ve had to prove people wrong my whole career,’ he says. 'If someone tells me I can’t do something, it motivates me to do it more. You look at all the great athletes, Tom Brady and that unwavering mentality to be the best. Maybe with me, because I’m a calm person and you don’t see the ego of some of these great players, it doesn’t mean I don’t want it as much as everyone else. It doesn’t mean I don’t put in the work and drive myself and everyone around me to be the best.

‘Getting released that early (by Arsenal) and proving them wrong. Proving my early coaches at Tottenham wrong, who I wasn’t playing as much under. Loan moves that didn’t go well. The World Cup in Qatar, missing that penalty was a really tough moment for me. After that, I scored the next 30 penalties! It’s the same thing, “I’m going to show them”, using all the negative stuff as motivation to push me to another level.’

Then there was Euro 2024, when Kane was substituted in the final defeat by Spain after an hour. The popular opinion went that his best days were behind him and England needed a new striker. He has since scored 25 goals from 27 international games. So much for the decline.

‘It was tough, getting taken off in a final,’ he says. ‘There was so much talk (before the final) around, “Maybe Harry shouldn't start”. I was like, “Well hang on a minute, I'm doing my best for the team here”.

‘I scored three goals and was joint for the Golden Boot. It wasn't like there were many other players doing crazy stuff that I wasn't doing. But from my own standards, I know I probably didn't quite reach the level that I could have. I don't think the team reached the level that we could have. After that, my position was under pressure. That motivated me to make sure that it wasn't. I was going to have to do even more to keep my place. From that moment, you've seen an improvement in me.’

Spend time with Kane, even just half an hour, and you realise he isn’t done yet.

’In football, you’ve never completed it,’ says the Bayern Munich star. ‘No matter what you’ve achieved, there is always a trophy that someone else has won or a goal record that someone else has. This is no time to rest. If anything, I've got better year on year, and the numbers have got better. While I'm feeling like this, why would I put any limit on myself? I'm just on the back of scoring 73 goals in one year, which is incredible, and I want to get 100 England goals as quickly as possible.

‘My biggest fear is finishing my career and thinking I could have done a bit more. I want to make sure that I cross every bridge and do everything possible so that, whenever that day comes, I can say, “I’ve done everything possible. I have this record, I don’t have this record, but it doesn’t matter, I can sleep well at night”.’

You could never accuse Kane of not giving his all. His ego, the best kind of ego, would never allow anything else. England's greatest player is the diva who makes only demands of himself.

#2015. ‘Looking back…’ – Alexander Isak speaks out over penalty controversy in defeat to Arsenal

Alexander Isak has spoken out about the controversial penalty incident in which he was involved during Liverpool’s defeat to Arsenal a fortnight ago.

Five minutes after Kai Havertz netted the only goal of the match, the Reds’ number 9 had his shirt pulled by Jurrien Timber inside the box, but neither on-field referee Andy Madley nor Stuart Attwell on VAR deemed it to have been a foul.

The transgression was unmistakably clear on replays, and the Premier League’s Key Match Incidents panel has since acknowledged that a spot kick should’ve been awarded.

Speaking to reporters whilst on international duty with Sweden, Isak was asked if he felt that he should’ve had a penalty.

He replied (Aftonbladet, via Liverpool Echo): “Yeah, looking back I suppose it does look that way, but when you’re in the moment, you don’t always perceive exactly what’s happening.

“I could feel myself being pulled a bit, but not to the extent that it appears later on. I was focused on scoring. It’s hard to try to score and then fall down at the same time. I was so locked in on the goal that I didn’t really register it.”

On whether he should’ve gone to ground to try and sway the referee, Isak said: “I don’t think there’s any need to embellish or go down on purpose. Sure, if I’d had a better read on the situation, I might have made sure the referee noticed it, that’s about all you can do, but I don’t believe you need to dive or exaggerate in situations like this.

“Perhaps it shouldn’t even matter that much, given that we have VAR and systems in place to make the decisive calls in these kinds of moments.”

Isak is absolutely right in saying that a penalty should’ve been awarded, and that he shouldn’t have to act unnaturally to convince the referee to give the decision in his team’s favour.

Andoni Iraola remarked after the game that a spot kick probably would’ve been given if the Liverpool striker had gone to ground, but the onus isn’t on players to sway the officials – it’s on the latter to get these big calls right, especially with recourse to VAR.

It feels as though the debate about officiating in the Premier League will continue indefinitely, with no discernible sign of an improvement in standards from Pro Ref figurehead Howard Webb.

It’s to Isak’s great credit that he’s given such a calm and measured verdict on the penalty incident when he and his team were so blatantly wronged. He’d have had every right to complain profusely about what happened; we’d suspect that many other players would’ve done so if they were in that situation.

He certainly hasn’t let it bother him in terms of his contributions on the pitch, with the 27-year-old scoring in Liverpool’s subsequent games against Fenerbahce and Crystal Palace to take his tally for the season to eight goals in 14 matches across all competitions.

That is, in fact, the best response to the injustice which was done against him Anfield two weeks ago.

#2011. Can Scott Parker Fix What Nuno Couldn’t? West Ham News

Following the international break, Saturday’s clash with Preston North End feels like a pivotal moment in West Ham’s season. The Hammers desperately need to start climbing the table, and while promotion remains within reach, time is quickly becoming a factor.

Promotion from the Championship is not won on reputation alone. West Ham began the season as the bookmakers’ favourites for automatic promotion, but that tag has quietly disappeared.

The dismissal of Nuno and the appointment of Scott Parker signalled a fresh start, although our new manager has had limited time with the squad before the break. What already seems evident, however, is that West Ham’s struggles stem from structural issues rather than shortcomings of individual players.

Kretinsky was not prepared to back Espirito Santo any longer -his tactics and playing style were not working

Parker will be fully aware of the challenges facing his side. The Championship is a division where possession statistics mean very little unless they are backed up by purpose, intensity and results.

Goals have not been the problem. Defensive frailties have been the far greater concern. Playing  Morato at left back never looked convincing, and Saturday’s team selection will be fascinating. With Kilman unavailable due to suspension, Parker must decide whether to pair Mavropanos with Golambekis or Morato.

The absence of a prolific, out-and-out goalscorer has also raised questions. Joel Piroe was recruited to fill that role and, on paper, the logic was sound. He is a proven Championship striker. Four goals and two assists in 14 appearances suggest he is moving in the right direction, but when compared to the division’s leading scorer, Will Lankshear, who has 13 goals, the gap is impossible to ignore.

Ironically, West Ham are the Championship’s leading scorers with 37 goals. Encouragingly, those goals are coming from all areas of the pitch rather than relying on a single player. Yet, there is one player, Jarrod Bowen who has been central to that success, contributing seven goals and leading the league’s assist charts with seven in fifteen matches.

He will go if the club don’t secure promotion, an inevitable outcome should the club not succeed this season.

Perhaps the biggest challenge for West Ham, is psychological.

West Ham arrived in the Championship expecting results to come naturally. As fans we expected an automatic promotion place.

At times this season, West Ham have looked weighed down by expectation. Instead of playing with the confidence of promotion contenders, the team have often appeared nervous and overly cautious, afraid of making costly mistakes.

Scott Parker’s biggest task may not be tactical at all. He must build a mentality centred on resilience and belief rather than entitlement.

If he can transform West Ham into a side that is more aggressive, more robust and better suited to the harsh realities of Championship football, promotion is still very much achievable.

If he cannot, the club’s stay in the second tier could last far longer than anyone at the London Stadium ever imagined. Saturday could be the first real indication of which path they are heading down.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

Sadly we have challenges throughout the club. Why not wait till the international break to change managers? Parker wasn’t going anywhere! Poor recruitment because every manager never seem to get the players they want and we, the supporters never seem to approve of any of the managers! I think it’s a little unfair to compare Piroe to Lankshear. The latter is first choice at his club and plays every game. You say Piroe has made 14 appearances but how many of those are starts and more importantly consecutive starts?

There are very significant doubts about the “shortcomings” of Hermansen, Kilman, Walker-Peters, Morato, Boiro, Scales, Magassa, Solomon, Piroe, Pablo, Castellanos; even our best “defender” , Mavropanos, is inconsistent & worrying at best. #2010. Liverpool Confidential: Why Will Wright is the breakout star of Reds academy - LEWIS STEELE reveals club's plans for 6ft 3in hat-trick hero, his rise from Euxton Villa to Anfield and why coaches believe he's Andoni Iraola's next big thing

Published: 12:00 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 16:17 EST, 11 November 2026

On Will Wright’s last two trips abroad, he has needed to check in some extra baggage on the return flight.

Two UEFA Youth League away games, two hat-tricks and a pair of match balls to go with them. It’s now 13 goals for the season for 18-year-old Wright after his treble in a 5-3 win at Fenerbahce last week, and he has earned a first England youth call-up to boot.

Another hat-trick in one of those three games for the Young Lions? You wouldn’t bet against it – but Wright is used to these rapid rises.

Eighteen months ago, the 6ft 3in striker signed for Liverpool on a Friday, passed his driving test at 8am the next morning and then played for the first team the day after in a friendly at Anfield.

Now, the former Salford City striker is the name on everyone’s lips around Kirkby – with many thinking he could be the next cab off the rank from Liverpool’s famed academy.

Will Wright has lit up the academy goal charts this season for Liverpool, scoring a pair of hat-tricks in the UEFA Youth League

The Under 19s captain struck a brilliant treble against Fenerbahce last week to take his season tally to 13

Wright was first spotted by Salford scouts when playing for local side Euxton Villa, a ninth-tier club who have two England internationals among their alumni in David Unsworth and Sam Johnstone. Wright’s father, Mark, coached at Euxton and is an ex-professional for Preston North End.

It was an unusual path as most future stars are normally signed up by their mid-teens but Wright had injury issues amid a growth spurt that took him to the lanky frame that now bullies defenders. He had heel issues and has worked with a specialist on fascia problems.

Wright made his Salford debut in an 8-0 FA Cup defeat by Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City in January 2025 but scouts had already been alerted by his 50-goal haul at youth level. Arsenal, led by then-academy chief Per Mertesacker, launched an aggressive approach to sign him.

At one point, Liverpool signalled to Wright and Salford that they were pulling out of the deal, given Arsenal’s interest was so advanced. But the Reds soon returned to prevent the Gunners signing their next ‘Wrighty’.

The deal was worth peanuts in the grand scheme of things, around £300,000. It is good money for League Two Salford, though, and they will be set for additional payments for first-team appearances, honours and future national team caps.

Wright, who has a younger brother and is a Nike athlete, is a throwback No9. It is easy to reach for comparisons to current players but the way he combines pace, power and prolific finishing is not too dissimilar to Erling Haaland.

He is a strong dribbler and scored a fantastic solo goal for Liverpool's Under 21s against Rochdale in the EFL Trophy in September, receiving possession on the touchline around halfway, tricking his way past two defenders and curling a sumptuous effort into the top corner.

He is the captain of the Under 19s team and I have watched him play live several times, including one game last season where he was clearly targeted by Atletico Madrid defenders. The striker was clattered, suffered a medial ligament injury and was sidelined for several months.

He is a strong dribbler and scored a fantastic solo goal for Liverpool's Under 21s against Rochdale in the EFL Trophy in September

Coaches have pinpointed hold-up play and heading as two things to work on, as well as instructing Wright not to ‘rise to the bait’ of bigger defenders who might try to ruffle him up

He has returned with a vengeance, with a hat-trick against LASK last month and then last week's effort against Fenerbahce. What impressed more in the latter was not his goals – one a penalty, the other two both true poachers’ finishes – but his assist.

Wright was on a hat-trick at the time but, instead of shooting, he played a ball to Finn Inglethorpe – son of academy director Alex – to score. Earlier, Wright and Josh Sonni-Lambie had argued over who was to take a penalty. Wright won the row and scored.

Under 21s boss Rob Page told the pair later that he would rather them show hunger to score and passion rather than shy away. Page is a huge fan of Wright and said: ‘There was a real maturity about his performance. One of the parts of the development for all the forwards is being unselfish in their actions.

‘As much as he wants to see the headlines and be successful himself, it is all about sharing that. Will has done that really well today with a hat-trick, a complete performance.’

Pressed on how far away Wright is from the first team, Page replied: ‘He doesn’t have to worry about that. Just bring the best version of yourself every day in training, give absolutely everything in games as he does. The rest will take care of itself.

‘He’s got a great support around him. His family are very supportive. Alex (Inglethorpe) is there to lean on, he’s got myself and Jay (Spearing, academy coach). He never gets carried away.’

Coaches have pinpointed hold-up play and heading as two things to work on, as well as instructing Wright not to ‘rise to the bait’ of bigger defenders who might try to ruffle him up. They have also worked on his off-the-ball runs to the back post.

So, what next? It is understood a January loan is being considered. Liverpool think toughening up Wright in a senior league could be a step worth taking, having used him in each of the last two pre-seasons. His agent was at the AXA Training Centre on Tuesday and there will be no shortage of clubs willing to take him on.

Liverpool think toughening up Wright in a senior league could be a step worth taking, having used him in each of the last two pre-seasons

Wright got six minutes off the bench against Como in a friendly at Anfield in August, coming on for Alexander Isak up front

Andoni Iraola will be consulted, too. He has called up the likes of Trey Nyoni, Lewis Koumas and Luke Chambers this season and is eager to use young stars.

Iraola is in frequent dialogue with youth staff such as Page, Inglethorpe, plus Luiz Fernando Iubel who is often cited as the ‘link’ between the academy and first team.

The Brazilian has been spotted at several academy games this term, including for Wright’s hat-trick in Turkey where Iubel sat alongside sporting director Julian Ward and loans manager Gary Probert.

Whether a first-team breakthrough comes now or in the future, the future for Wright looks bright.

Dominik Szoboszlai’s participation with Hungary this week remains in the balance with the national team doing all they can to get their captain fit for crunch games.

The Hungarians take on Georgia and Northern Ireland in must-win Nations League matches – and may have to go without their star man. Szoboszlai hurt his knee in the win at Crystal Palace and, after an injury-hit six weeks, could do with a rest.

But he will try his best to be fit for national team duty and a decision will not be made until the 11th hour.

It comes after Virgil van Dijk pulled out of Dutch duty with a minor muscle issue. It is believed he has been managing the problem for at least a month and was surprised to be substituted on to the field against LASK — which might explain the team conceding three after he came on!

Virgil van Dijk (left) has pulled out of international duty and Dominik Szoboszlai (right) could be set to follow him

Confidential readers will recall our musings on Harvey Elliott a fortnight ago, with Valencia sources telling us that the La Liga outfit might consider cancelling his loan in January.

The English midfielder had struggled in Spain for fitness and form. He was then sent off against Villarreal but, as we reported, Valencia would give him another chance to prove his worth.

He has started well, scoring a free-kick in what was his first start for any club in 285 days. It was part of a notable 6-0 win in the Copa del Rey.

Elliott ran over to fans and put his arms aloft appearing to apologise, which adds to his comments a week ago about the red card where he said: ‘I made a mistake and I’m truly sorry. It won’t happen again.’

Milan entered the international break with a much-needed victory against Genoa, but it wasn’t the easiest result of the season. After a disappointing defeat to Ferencvaros – which extended the midweek run of defeats – they couldn’t afford to drop points, and they succeeded, even if it wasn’t without flaw.

We indeed lost against Milan, but we lost ‘well.’ We didn’t deserve it. Three or four weeks ago, the latest results seemed like a pipe dream. I thank the players, staff, and my club for giving me faith and patience at a time when other clubs wouldn’t have had it.

“They remembered how good we did last year. I’m happy to have emerged from a difficult period and to be Genoa’s coach; I’m really happy there.”

“I’m passionate about the fans and the supporters. I’m part of a club that, in terms of fan base, is among the best in Europe. I’m passionate; I don’t punch a clock. “Genoa is full of Genoese fans who remind you every second how much they love their club, the pride of being the top club in Italy. West Ham United’s window of opportunity to acquire their rented home for next to nothing appears to be fading. With £20 million of losses each year, the ground is a massive white elephant with the main tenant paying next to nothing for it’s bullet proof lease.

Former vice Chair Karren Brady, say what you like about her,  did at least negotiate the deal of the century giving West Ham a rock solid indestructible tenancy for generations to come. As the club were relegated, so the rent diminished leaving the owners to pick up the tab for West Ham’s failure on the pitch: An estimated £2.5 million each year is added to the tax payer burden thanks to the clause existing to reduce costs when West Ham dropped out of the Premier League.

According to London.stadium.com that effort has paid dividends:

Meaning the revenue which can be generated from the Stadium will be significantly higher, theoretically at least increasing its value and likely heading off West Ham’s options of acquiring it for next to nothing. Possibly.

West Ham’s London Stadium at night: There’ll be more events, louder music and bigger attendances – still won’t make a profit though. Just saying.

However the huge maintenance costs and temporary nature of the upper part of the structure means that even with consent for more events, bigger attendances and louder music, London Stadium is never going to become a lucrative, marketable venue in it’s current configuration.

Someone is going to have to spend hundreds of millions of pounds on fixing it: Like a giant pass-the-parcel game with a huge ticking time bomb of debt at the core of the fancy wrapping, neither West Ham nor the owners want to be left holding the bill when the music stops.

The difference is, the status quo favours the club, not the Greater London Authority who, as it stands, will find it pretty near impossible to turn a profit even with new approvals granted and new events lined up. And as every year passes, the need to spend big, big money on maintenance grows greater. In this instance, West Ham’s board biding their time and kicking it into the long grass for a few years yet is probably the shrewdest course of action. From the football club’s perspective.
