#1976. Japan vs Paraguay - prediction, team news, lineups

By Ben Sully | 16 Nov 2026 00:29, Last updated: 17 Nov 2026 18:00

Japan and Paraguay will conclude their respective 2026 schedules when they face off in Tuesday's friendly in Singapore.

The Samurai Blue pulled off a thrilling win over Brazil last time out, while Paraguay cruised to a commanding victory over Singapore in their most recent outing.

Japan head into Tuesday's fixture in fine form, having lost just one of their previous 16 internationals.

Their only defeat in that period came in the Round of 32 tie against Brazil at the 2026 World Cup, which saw them spurn a leading position in a narrow 2-1 defeat.

After conceding a late winner in that contest, Hajime Moriyasu's side managed to exact an element of revenge with a stoppage-time winner of their own in Saturday's friendly against Brazil.

The Samurai Blue looked to have wasted another strong position after Takefusa Kubo and Keito Nakamura saw their efforts cancelled out by a Vinicius Junior brace, before Coventry City's Tatsuhiro Sakamoto turned the game back in Japan's favour with a 91st-minute goal.

Sakamoto's effort made it two wins in Japan's last three head-to-head meetings with Brazil, while making it five games without defeat since their World Cup elimination.

Japan should fancy their chances of extending their unbeaten run with a win, having won four of their previous five meetings with Paraguay (D1) since losing on penalties in the last 16 of the 2010 World Cup.

After eventually being eliminated in the quarter-finals in 2010, Paraguay had to wait 16 years until their next appearance in football's biggest tournament.

La Albirroja certainly made an impact at the 2026 World Cup, advancing to the knockout rounds before eliminating Germany on penalties in the Round of 32.

However, their run ultimately came to an end in a feisty last-16 clash against France, with Kylian Mbappe's 70th-minute penalty proving decisive as Paraguay fell to a narrow 1-0 loss.

Gustavo Alfaro's side have since made a positive return to action with three consecutive wins against Bolivia, Colombia and Singapore.

Gustavo Caballero netted a brace as Paraguay cruised to a 4-1 success in their most recent outing against Singapore, representing just the third time La Albirroja have scored two or more goals in 2026.

Their strength has ultimately been at the opposite end of the pitch, having conceded more than one goal in just two of their 11 games in the current calendar year.

Japan have announced that Daichi Kamada has been allowed to return to Crystal Palace after playing 72 minutes in the win over Brazil.

Ko Itakura, Yukinari Sugawara and Kaishu Sano are among those who could start if Moriyasu opts to rotate his side.

Sakamoto, Takumi Minamino and Koki Ogawa could come in to freshen up Japan's attack for Tuesday's friendly.

As for Paraguay, Alfaro is expected to make wholesale changes after naming an experimental XI for the win over Singapore.

Juan Jose Caceres, Gustavo Gomez and Omar Alderete are likely to come into the back four for Paraguay's final outing of 2026.

Diego Gomez, Miguel Almiron and Julio Enciso are also among those who are expected to start against Japan.

Suzuki; Sugawara, Seko, Itakura, Ito; Ka Sano, Tanaka; Sakamoto, Minamino, Nakamura; Ogawa

Gill; Caceres, G. Gomez, Alderete, Maidana; Cuenca, Galarza, D. Gomez, Almiron; Benitez, Enciso

Japan will be full of confidence after pulling off a notable win over Brazil, and while we think they will claim another victory on Tuesday, we believe the scoreline will be close against a Paraguay team that is usually a tough side to break down.

#1974. Cardinale says MSE will give Milan ‘financial muscle’ and reiterates: “I will never sell”

Gerry Cardinale has commented on the launch of AC Milan’s new holding company, Milan Sports & Entertainment (MSE), stating that he will never sell the club.

Yesterday, it was confirmed that RedBird had launched the new holding company to ‘consolidate RedBird’s Milan-based investments in sports, infrastructure, and entertainment’. From the new stadium to the NBA Europa project, there are big plans for the company.

Brett Yormark has been appointed as the CEO of MSE after impressing as the Commissioner of the Big 12 Conference (college sports), labelling it ‘an honour’ to get the position. It doesn’t mean that we will see less of Cardinale though, quite the opposite.

In an interview with Gazzetta dello Sport this morning, Cardinale outlined exactly what he wants to achieve with MSE and explained why he will never sell the club. Silvio Berlusconi 2.0, as he calls it, with the goal of taking Milan back to the very top.

Cardinale, what benefits will AC Milan gain from the holding company?

“The driving force behind deals like this is to provide AC Milan with the financial muscle needed to compete in the transfer market and secure the best players in the world.

“I will transform the club’s financial profile with the resources that will come from the stadium, the San Donato Arena, and the other activities we are working on with NBA Europe.

“I’m doing everything I can to ensure that, when we want a player, no one can tell me, ‘You can’t sign him because you can’t afford him.’ Currently, only Premier League clubs are able to invest such sums and secure top players.

“If I want to bring AC Milan back to the top of European competition, not just in Italy, we need to figure out how to compete with the world’s top clubs.”

This project confirms that your commitment to Milan is long-term…

“Yes. I will never sell AC Milan. Never. And this is a project to get them back to winning ways. I’m not willing to tolerate it taking a long time to achieve this. I want to do it as soon as possible. We’ll see how quickly…

“My goal is to consistently win Scudetti and, of course, return to the Champions League. Milan Sports & Entertainment represents the foundation to make all this possible.”

The connection with Milan deserves a separate mention: RedBird and the city are now even more connected…

“This is the legacy we will leave in Milan. The stadium, obviously, represents a huge legacy that will transform our financial profile, but then there’s also the San Donato development project and the rest.

“If we want AC Milan to become great again, we need to close the revenue gap with the Premier League clubs. When I bought the club four years ago, I used the expression ‘Berlusconi 2.0’ and no one understood what I meant. Now perhaps we are starting to see it.”

“Everyone thought I was making an arrogant, self-centred comparison between me and Berlusconi, but that wasn’t my point. What I was trying to explain was that, just as Berlusconi transformed AC Milan and Serie A, we want to be able, through our ownership, to lead the club into a new era.

“We need to do it in the same way Berlusconi did, albeit in a modern way. I’m used to working a certain way because that’s how I do things, at the highest levels worldwide and in America.”

Could your “recipe” also be valid for Serie A?

“Of course, even for Serie A. In my opinion, it wouldn’t have been a good deal to sell 30% of the league’s international TV rights when JP Morgan made that offer. That’s not how Serie A can return to the top of Europe.

“It needs to be done through business planning and by creating every opportunity to generate new revenue. Like we will do with Milan Sports & Entertainment.

“We will be the first to build a stadium since 2011, and that’s a huge achievement. I started working on it when I bought AC Milan, and finally… the right time has arrived.”

Do you think others will follow you on this path?

“No. Some may do it, others may not. We know what it takes to innovate and change. To avoid continuing to practice Einstein’s definition of insanity, according to which everyone wants a different outcome, but doesn’t want to do anything different to get it.”

How long do you think it will take to complete the other projects that will be part of the new holding company?

“I think the NBA is negotiating with the Euroleague, but one way or another, if they can’t reach an agreement, NBA Europe will still launch. Perhaps the first batch of new franchises for Europe will be announced at the end of the year or in early 2027.

“We will see when that happens… We own the land in San Donato, and if I’m granted the Milan franchise, I will be able to start construction fairly quickly because we already have planning permission for a 20,000-seat arena.

“We will also continue to explore opportunities and hold discussions within the tennis world and to organise a tournament in Milan. Finally, we are already making progress in building and launching a hospitality and facility management company.”

Does your plan include organising and managing hospitality services for other clubs’ stadiums as well, not just the new San Siro?

“Yes, the model is the company I created in 2009, called Legends Hospitality. I created it with the New York Yankees and the Dallas Cowboys. Now that company is worth several billion dollars.

“We not only sell premium seats, suites, merchandise, and hospitality, food, and beverage services for Yankee Stadium and Cowboys Stadium, but also for other clubs. I would like to adopt the same model here, probably in partnership with another club.”

Not many football clubs in the world have established an organisation like the one you are leading…

“Exactly. My ambition is to compete with the best clubs in the world. I want to do so thanks to my global vision of the world of sports and entertainment.

“There aren’t many multi-sports platforms in the world that also own some of their own facilities, and we want to add AC Milan to that list. To compete with them and then be better.”

In an effort to generate new revenue, are you also considering a tour for AC Milan next summer? Will that still be Australia or the United States?

“We have already discussed it with Amorim, and I will just tell you that if we play friendlies abroad, they will be in the United States next summer. If we do… We haven’t decided yet, and the decision will be up to Ruben.

“It will depend on what’s best for the team: playing friendlies abroad must add value to the group, not bring in a couple of million for the club. Those extra two million will no longer be our goal, as they were under the previous management. That won’t happen again under this ownership.

“Everything we organise in terms of friendlies will be carefully considered with our coach. Every move. And we won’t participate in tours organised by others. We put our players first. We want to help them prepare well to win. That’s our goal, and we aim to achieve it as soon as possible.”

Gerry is right. You are wrong. Look it up.

The English Premiere League makes about FOUR TIMES as much money in TV broadcast rights as Serie A does – €4.6 billion per season (£3.84 billion – £1.68 billion domestic, £2.17 billion international).

Serie A’s TV broadcast rights give it €1.144 billion per season (€894 million domestic, €250 million international)

Total stadium revenue among all the clubs in the English Premier League is also about 2.3 x higher than total stadium revenue for all the clubs in Serie A – over £1billion per season in the EPL (€1.3 billion) compared with €435.4 million per season in Serie A.

It was not always this way. In the 1980s, English football was beset with old, rotting, unsafe stadiums, hooliganism, and low TV revenues.

In 1992, the First Division clubs broke away from the rest of the English Football League (EFL) to form the Premiere League, and began negotiating TV contracts on their own, as well as embarking on a program of enlarging and upgrading their football stadiums. The richest teams began building completely new, large modern stadiums with premium suites, etc.

Meanwhile, nothing much has changed in Italy – most of the stadiums remain municipal owned and small and old.

Ticket prices in the EPL are also generally on average about twice as expensive as in Italy.

So yeah, Serie A had its glory days in the 1990s, as wealthy magnates like Berlusconi infused their personal wealth into their clubs. I remember Fox carried Serie A football on TV in the United States back then. If you wanted to watch the English Premiere League, it was a bit of a struggle to find the matches on TV in the U.S back in the 1990s.

All that changed as the Premiere League steadily built up its international marketing and negotiated ever improved TV contracts. It began to require clubs that were promoted up to the EPL to upgrade their stadiums to meet a certain minimum seating capacity.

And so, today, when Italians complain about how Italy and Serie A can no longer compete with the English Premiere League for the best players, how the EPL hugely overpays for all its star players, the reason is that the EPL makes a $HIT TON MORE MONEY than Serie A does, across the board, in TV income (the biggest factor for the entire league), and stadium income.

That’s why Gerry wanted a new and better stadium, and why he has often talked about Serie A needing to do better marketing and improve its TV contracts.

You can’t get the best players in the world if you can’t compete financially with the richest and most watched football league in the world, which happens to be the English Premiere League right now.

Here in the US, EPL matches are carried by NBC Sports by subscription (about $130-$200 a year). NBC pays the Premiere League $450 million per season to carry English football on TV in the USA.

Serie A matches are carried by Paramount/CBS in the USA (a $90 per year subscription – it went up from $60 after the Ellison Oligarchy mergers). CBS had been paying Serie A $75.8 million per year for those TV rights. However, Serie A with its great marketing and negotiating expertise was unable to improve or renew that contract and so Serie A is currently just going year to year with CBS and getting less than $30 million a year.

Do you see the difference now in the major sources of income between the Premiere League and Serie A??

So yeah, absolutely, Gerry is right to complain about needing to get Serie A some better negotiators and marketers to improve on its TV contracts.

#1973. Liberia vs Cape Verde - prediction, team news, lineups

By Nsidibe Akpan | 16 Nov 2026 00:32, Last updated: 17 Nov 2026 18:11

Bottom-placed Liberia host Cape Verde in a Group K fixture of 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifying at the Samuel Kanyon Doe Sports Complex in Monrovia on Tuesday.

The first leg in Praia on November 13 finished 4-2 to Cape Verde, which lifted the Blue Sharks to three points in third place in a group where only the top two qualify.

The Lone Stars sit bottom of Group K with no points from three matches, having scored three goals and conceded eight, a goal difference of -5 that leaves them six points behind second-placed Rwanda with nine still available.

Mohammed Adil Erradi, the Belgian-Moroccan appointed on a three-year contract on May 18, has yet to win a competitive match as Liberia coach, and a group calling itself the Concerned Stakeholders for Liberian Football Development demanded his dismissal on October 9, according to the Liberian Observer, citing a salary budgeted at US$98,450 a year.

The campaign opened with a 3-1 defeat in Kigali on September 25, where Sylvanus Nimely scored the only Liberian goal, and four days later Mali won 1-0 at this ground through Martial Tia’s 79th-minute strike after goalkeeper Tommy Songo pulled out of the starting line-up during the warm-up.

In Praia on November 13 Liberia trailed 3-1 after 43 minutes, with Franklin Nyenetue’s 36th-minute equaliser cancelled out two minutes later by a corner-kick header from Dje Tavares, before Ayouba Kosiah converted a stoppage-time penalty to set the final score at 4-2.

Liberia’s back three of Jamal Arago, Sampson Dweh and Emmanuel Fully conceded to a scramble in their own box, a corner and a marking lapse in the first leg, and the defence has now shipped eight goals in three qualifiers, an average of 2.67 per match.

The head-to-head record leans away from the hosts, as Liberia have lost their last three meetings with Cape Verde (2-1 in Accra on October 7, 2021, 1-0 in Mindelo on October 10, 2021, and 4-2 on November 13), although both of their wins in the series came in Monrovia, 3-0 in July 2000 and 1-0 on June 5, 2011.

A post shared by Liberia Men's National Teams (@lbr_lonestar)

Cape Verde arrive third in Group K on three points with a goal difference of -1 (six scored, seven conceded), and a win in Monrovia would take them to six, level with the total currently held by second-placed Rwanda, who host Mali in Kigali at the same 7pm GMT kickoff.

The Blue Sharks drew all three of their World Cup group matches in June (0-0 against Spain, 2-2 against Uruguay and 0-0 against Saudi Arabia) to reach the Round of 32 on their tournament debut, where Argentina beat them 3-2 after extra time on July 3, a 111th-minute own goal from Diney Borges settling it after Deroy Duarte and Sidny Lopes Cabral had pulled Cape Verde level twice.

Bubista then left to coach Moroccan club RS Berkane, and Humberto Bettencourt, his assistant for six years, was promoted on August 19, with his first two qualifiers producing a 3-1 defeat at Mali on September 25 and a 2-1 home defeat to Rwanda on September 29.

Those results extended a winless run to six matches, counting the World Cup (three draws and three defeats), which ended in Praia when Ayoni Santos, Dje Tavares, Dailon Livramento and substitute Derensili Sanches Fernandes scored in the 4-2 win, Bettencourt’s first victory in charge.

Cape Verde have conceded in all three of their qualifiers, seven goals at 2.33 per match, compared with five conceded across four World Cup matches, two of which were clean sheets against Spain and Saudi Arabia.

Bettencourt brought in six players for the double-header, among them David Moreira, Yuran Fernandes, Leandro Andrade, Ieltsin Camoes and Sanches Fernandes, and three of the four scorers in Praia (Santos, Tavares and Sanches Fernandes) were finding the net for the senior side for the first time.

Liberia Africa Cup of Nations Qualifying form:

Cape Verde Africa Cup of Nations Qualifying form:

Liberia captain Oscar Dorley, the Al-Taawoun midfielder, is out with a hamstring injury and was left out of Erradi’s 24-man squad, while goalkeeper Derrick Julu of Niger Tornadoes was recalled to replace Songo, who has not featured since withdrawing from the Mali line-up on September 29.

Julu replaced Ashley Williams at half time in Praia, and Erradi said afterwards that Williams, who had played well against Mali, was not at his best, which points to Julu starting in goal on Tuesday.

Nyenetue, who plays for Ranheim, scored the equaliser in Praia and was replaced by William Gibson after 64 minutes with no injury reported.

Without Dorley, Nohan Kenneh and Solomon Tweh are the likeliest holding pairing in a four-man midfield that also used Edward Ledlum and Divine Teah of Slavia Prague, with Sampson Dweh of Viktoria Plzen anchoring the back three.

For the visitors, defender Wagner Pina, who had joined the training camp in Portugal, did not travel to Cape Verde for the first leg, and Bettencourt wished him a quick recovery.

The 26-man squad named on November 4 includes Vozinha, 40, defenders Logan Costa and Lopes Cabral, midfielder Jamiro Monteiro and 36-year-old captain Ryan Mendes, although Lopes Cabral was replaced at half time in Praia by Steven Moreira and the reason has not been given.

Bettencourt could keep the 4-1-4-1 that scored four in Praia, with Deroy Duarte shielding the back four, and he used all five substitutions there (Moreira, Monteiro, Laros Duarte, Sanches Fernandes and Camoes), which leaves a bench that is already familiar with the plan.

Julu; Fully, Dweh, Jamal, Nimely; Ledlum, Tweh, Kenneh, Nyenetue; Teah, Kosiah

Vozinha; J. Paulo, Diney, Costa, L. Cabral; D. Duarte; Mendes, Tavares, Santos, Varela; Livramento

The first leg showed where this tie will be decided, as Liberia conceded to a scramble in their own box, a corner and a marking lapse inside 43 minutes, and with Dorley absent and Erradi having already changed goalkeepers at half time, he has fewer ways to repair that in four days than Bettencourt has to exploit it again.

Liberia deserve credit for scoring twice in Praia and for restricting Mali to a 79th-minute winner on the synthetic surface at this ground, and both of their wins over Cape Verde came in Monrovia, but the latter of them is 15 years old and Cape Verde’s own record of conceding in every qualifier gives the hosts a route to one goal, which is why 1-2 is a better call than a repeat of the four-goal margin.

A Cape Verde win would lift them to six points, which only equals Rwanda’s tally if the Amavubi lose to Mali in Kigali on the same evening, so Bettencourt’s side cannot treat the second leg as a formality.

#1972. Watch: Camarda scores for Italy’s U21 side in 2-1 win against France

Francesco Camarda got on target for Italy’s U21 side last night as they beat France by two goals to one, bagging the opener.

It has been a tough season for Camarda so far. After a pre-season and summer that seemed to promise consistent playing time this season, the youngster has only racked up 119 minutes on the pitch between Serie A and the Europa League.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

No goals have been scored either, which is obviously never ideal for a striker looking to grow. A loan move appears to be on the cards, but the January window isn’t for another month and a half, so a confidence boost cannot come quickly enough. Luckily, he got one last night.

Italy U21 played a friendly against France in Laval last night and Camarda managed to get the opener in the game. After picking up a good position, the striker veered off into the centre and found the open space in France’s defence.

Camarda received the ball from Matteo Dagasso and while it looked for a split second like the pass was overhit, he got on the end of it and found the back of the net. Once again, as we have seen with Milan this season too, his movement was crucial in creating the chance.

Let’s see what happens in the coming weeks, but perhaps he can get some more chances by Amorim and finally score his first goal with the red and black shirt.

#1971. Jordan vs Australia - prediction, team news, lineups

By Saikat Mandal | 16 Nov 2026 00:33, Last updated: 16 Nov 2026 08:05

Jordan and Australia will face off in a rare November international friendly at Suheim Bin Hamad Stadium in Doha on Tuesday.

The home side are striving for consistency following their group-stage exit from the 2026 World Cup, while Australia will be looking to make it back-to-back away victories.

Jordan may have fallen short of the group-stage hurdle at their first-ever World Cup, but they still produced some memorable moments for their supporters.

Despite suffering a 3-1 defeat to Austria in their opening game, Ali Olwan's stunning strike remains fresh in the memory.

Jordan failed to win either of their remaining matches against Algeria and Argentina, but they showed no shortage of fighting spirit before their World Cup campaign came to an end.

Badou Zaki's side are now without a win in their last 10 matches and have recorded two draws since the tournament.

The Chivalrous Ones played out a 1-1 draw against Syria in their first match after the World Cup in September before being held to a goalless stalemate by Venezuela in October, extending their winless run through two underwhelming friendlies.

In contrast, Australia enjoyed a memorable tournament, reaching the knockout stages despite being drawn in a difficult group.

Tony Popovic's side stunned many with a 2-0 victory over a strong Turkey outfit in their opening match.

They subsequently lost 2-0 to the USA, but a goalless draw was enough to secure their passage into the knockout rounds, where they suffered a 4-2 penalty shootout defeat to Egypt after the match finished 1-1 in normal time.

Australia faced Brazil twice in international friendlies after the World Cup, drawing 1-1 in the first encounter before losing 4-2 in the return fixture.

However, they head into this contest with renewed confidence after thrashing Qatar 3-0 earlier this week, with all three goals arriving in the first half.

Zaki has a fully fit squad at his disposal, and it will be interesting to see which combination he opts for.

Abdallah Al-Fakhouri could retain his place in goal, although Alec Samir featured in the 1-1 draw against Syria.

World Cup hero Mousa Al-Tamari is expected to lead the attack alongside Olwan and veteran forward Mahmoud Al-Mardi.

Australia, meanwhile, are missing several key players, with Cameron Burgess ruled out by a cruciate ligament injury and Jordan Bos also sidelined with a knee problem.

The Socceroos are also without skipper Mathew Ryan and fellow veterans Jackson Irvine and Milos Degenek, plus midfielder Aiden O'Neill, but it unclear whether they made themselves unavailable for safety reasons.

Diesel Herrington, Thomas Waddingham and Sam Klein are new call-ups, while striker Kusini Yengi joins brother Tete Yengi, while goalkeepers Joe Gauci and Tom Glover have been recalled.

Al-Fakhouri; Badawi, Nasib, Rousan, Taha; Sadeh, Al-Rawabdeh, Qashi; Tamari, Olwan, Al-Mardi

Beach; Kasey Bos, Herrington, Souttar, Circati, Italiano; McGree, Metcalfe, Okon-Engstler; Irankunda, Yengi

Jordan will be desperate to secure their first victory since 2025 and should fancy their chances against an Australian side missing several key players. However, the visitors will be keen to end the international break unbeaten, and we expect an entertaining contest to finish level.

#1970. Report: How Ronald Araujo, Barcelona and Liverpool feel about prospective permanent transfer

Reports from Spain have hinted that there’s a strong chance of Ronald Araujo signing for Liverpool permanently in 2027.

The Uruguayan defender is on loan at Anfield from Barcelona for this season, with the deal including a purchase option reportedly worth £47m.

The 27-year-old has been one of the Reds’ standout players in the first three months of the campaign, making the right-back berth his own despite playing most of his career at centre-back, and it’s been reported that he and his family are very happy and comfortable on Merseyside.

According to Marca, the Liverpool hierarchy are ‘seriously considering’ taking up the option to sign Araujo permanently and would even be willing to do so immediately, but that clause can’t be activated until the end of this season.

The report adds that ‘everything indicates’ that the defender would be prepared to join the Reds outright if the Merseyside club were to push for a permanent transfer.

Barcelona aren’t considering a return to Camp Nou for the Uruguayan, with an acceptance that they’re powerless to bring him back if LFC were to pay the purchase clause, and it’s deemed ‘highly unlikely’ that he’d revert to his parent club from next summer.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

With the Catalan club not necessarily resigned to their fate, but realising that they don’t hold the balance of power over Araujo, it feels increasingly as though he could become a Liverpool player outright in 2027.

Considering the all-action performances that the Uruguay international has been putting in at Anfield, and that we could lose the experience of Virgil van Dijk and Joe Gomez from our defence if neither sign new contracts, the Reds would be foolish not to try and activate the purchase option.

The 27-year-old seems quite happy to remain on Merseyside for the long-term, by all accounts, and Liverpool would buy him in the knowledge that he’s already proven he can thrive in the Premier League.

If he maintains the performance levels he’s shown so far at LFC throughout a full season, then £47m would seem a very fair outlay for Araujo, who’s helped to stabilise what had been a highly volatile right-back position in our line-up.

It’s frustrating in one sense that we have to wait until the end of the campaign to activate the purchase option, but unless there’s a major plot twist between now and May, we’re confident that a permanent transfer will ultimately be completed and he’ll be a Liverpool player outright in a few months’ time.

#1969. Poland vs Sweden - prediction, team news, lineups

By Anthony Nolan | 16 Nov 2026 01:18, Last updated: 17 Nov 2026 19:02

Fighting for a chance at survival in UEFA Nations League B, Poland will welcome Group B4 winners Sweden to Tarczynski Arena on Tuesday.

The Eagles are under pressure, though the Blue and Yellow have already clinched top spot and could be caught off guard.

Jan Urban's Poland have endured a dire campaign so far, and the best they can hope for at this stage is to survive by avoiding the League B/C playoffs.

The Eagles only required a draw against Romania last time out to secure their place in League B for next term, but they were beaten 2-1 in Bucharest on Saturday.

That defeat has left Urban's side third in Group B4 with four points to their name, just one clear of Romania ahead of the final matchday.

Knowing that victory for their rivals could force them into the relegation playoffs, Poland will be fearing a clash against in-form Sweden, especially after losing three of their last four outings.

However, the hosts will take heart from the fact they are unbeaten on home soil during this group stage, having drawn 0-0 with Bosnia-Herzegovina on September 25, before thrashing Romania 6-0 a week later.

Meanwhile, Graham Potter's Sweden are yet to taste defeat in Group B4, and are set to play League A football next term following an excellent campaign.

The Blue and Yellow held on to beat Bosnia-Herzegovina 3-2 on Saturday, racing into a three-goal lead courtesy of a fifth-minute opener from Borussia Dortmund's Daniel Svensson and a pair of penalties from Arsenal's Viktor Gyokeres, but conceded twice in a tense second half.

That performance fits Sweden's pattern, considering they have scored in the first 20 minutes during six of their last seven Nations League clashes, while 13 of their past 15 matches have seen both sides find the back of the net.

Regardless, securing their fourth win in five games has Potter's men top of the group with 13 points, five clear of the second-placed Dragons and nine above third-placed Poland.

The Blue and Yellow may no longer be under pressure, but they will be keen to end on a positive note, and having won eight of their last nine meetings with Poland, supporters will be looking forward to another triumph on Tuesday.

Poland will be without Porto centre-back Jakub Kiwior, who is suspended due to accumulating yellow cards, while Aston Villa right-back Matty Cash is a doubt with a leg problem and goalkeeper Kamil Grabara is sidelined with a cruciate ligament injury.

In their absence, Kacper Potulski could be joined by Tomasz Kedziora at the heart of the hosts' defence, flanked by Arkadiusz Pyrka and Oskar Kubiak at full-back in front of shot-stopper Bartlomiej Dragowski.

Elsewhere, Inter Milan midfielder Piotr Zielinski is unavailable due to illness, though Sebastian Szymanski and Wiktor Nowak should be on hand to start in the centre of the park.

As for Sweden, they are missing Tottenham Hotspur midfielder Lucas Bergvall (knee) and Lech Poznan winger Patrik Walemark (muscle).

With that in mind, expect to see Fulham's Hugo Larsson and Brighton and Hove Albion's Yasin Ayari line up in midfield, while Anthony Elanga and Sebastian Nanasi provide width.

Liverpool striker Alexander Isak will partner Viktor Gyokeres up top on Tuesday, with the latter hoping to add to his brace from last time out.

Dragowski; Pyrka, Potulski, Kedziora, Kubiak; Regula, Szymanski, Nowak, Zalewski; Lewandowski, Swiderski

Johansson; Svensson, Lagerbielke, Lindelof, Gudmundsson; Elanga, Larsson, Ayari, Nanasi; Gyokeres, Isak

Poland are sure to be feeling the pressure from Romania on Tuesday, and they will be keen to confirm their survival without relying on results elsewhere.

However, Sweden have dominated the head-to-head clashes between these nations, and are likely to continue that trend in midweek.

#1967. Mary Fowler was offered a record $1million to return home and reunite with Nathan Cleary - but she said no

Published: 21:52 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 21:57 EST, 11 November 2026

A reported record-breaking pay offer and the chance to live closer to Nathan Cleary were not enough to bring Mary Fowler back to Australia.

The Matildas star remains at Manchester City after a reported $1million offer emerged as part of an ambitious plan to recruit Australian sport’s glamour couple to two clubs under the same ownership umbrella.

The proposal could have offered a solution to the long-distance relationship that keeps their careers on opposite sides of the world.

For battling NRL franchise Wests Tigers, it was an extraordinary bid to prise one of rugby league’s biggest names away from Penrith.

According to News Corp, Tigers owner Holman Barnes Group proposed a combined package worth $9million, including a $1million marquee contract for Fowler to join the Central Coast Mariners women’s team.

The group had acquired the Mariners women’s side, opening the door to a recruitment pitch spanning two sports.

Mary Fowler remains at Manchester City despite a reported $1million offer to return to Australian football

A proposed recruitment package would have brought Fowler to the Central Coast Mariners and Cleary to Wests Tigers

Fowler returned to Australia in October to support Cleary following two operations

Under the reported proposal, Cleary would have joined the Tigers and Fowler would have returned to NSW on what would be the highest salary in A-League Women history.

But the blockbuster homecoming did not materialise.

Should athletes choose love or loyalty to their teams when faced with life-changing offers?

Panthers chairman Greg Alexander later explained that the damage, while confronting, could have been worse.

Cleary has since reportedly passed up another offer to remain with the club where he won four consecutive premierships.

The NRL expansion club the PNG Chiefs proposed a package worth up to $8.4million over three years, according to News Corp.

#1964. ‘Go and do it’ – Jamie Carragher issues January transfer plea to Liverpool chiefs

Jamie Carragher has urged Liverpool to be active in the January transfer window if ‘a certain type’ of player becomes attainable.

The Reds have made some major mid-season signings in the past, with Virgil van Dijk, Daniel Sturridge, Luis Suarez, Philippe Coutinho and Luis Diaz all joining in the winter months, but they haven’t entered the January market for an immediate new addition since landing Cody Gakpo nearly four years ago.

The window will open in just over six weeks’ time, so speculation over prospective new arrivals will no doubt intensify in the lead-up to New Year’s, and Carragher feels that his former club must be proactive if they spot the right market opportunity.

Speaking on The Overlap Fan Debate, the ex-Liverpool defender said: “For me, this season for [Andoni] Iraola is about making sure we’re in a position for next season to really challenge for the title, so I think every transfer window is rightly important.

“The areas on the pitch for Liverpool that still stand out for me – and we’ve got Hugo Ekitike to come back as well, so that’ll fix the back-up for Alexander Isak, or maybe play alongside Isak – is the full-back area.

“If there’s a left-back, they’ve got to go and do it in January. Or a midfield player, a certain type of midfield player. It’s not about what we did with [Jurgen] Klopp, where we’d wait for the summer, because this feels like it’s the here and now.”

One thing the Reds have proven quite adept at in previous Januarys is making a late surge to snare a mid-season signing, like they did when stealing in for Diaz in 2022 and Gakpo the following winter.

It’s notable that the Dutchman was signed when Julian Ward was Liverpool’s sporting director, and he’s now back in that job title for a second spell, having shown in the past that he’s prepared to pounce for the right opportunity.

Carragher’s reservations about the full-back berths are understandable. Both Jeremie Frimpong and Conor Bradley on the right have been hampered by injury issues, while Kostas Tsimikas hasn’t been able to provide stern competition for Milos Kerkez on the other flank.

LFC won’t enter the January market for the sake of it and won’t be swayed by external opinion, no matter how voluble it might be, but that isn’t to say that they definitely won’t bring in a new signing or two during the winter window.

Liverpool’s transfer strategy could also be swayed by what happens over the coming weeks, and whether they go into the New Year with Andoni Iraola worryingly light in some positions.

Carragher is spot-on about one thing – if there’s a smart deal to be done in January, then Ward must swoop in straight away rather than biding his time for next summer.

#1962. Bosnia-Herzegovina vs Romania - prediction, team news, lineups

By Anthony Nolan | 16 Nov 2026 02:26, Last updated: 17 Nov 2026 19:08

Romania will be battling for survival in UEFA Nations League B on Tuesday, when they travel to face Bosnia-Herzegovina at Stadion Bilino Polje.

The Dragons have already secured second place in Group B4, and are up against a Tricolorii team that need to win.

Sergej Barbarez's Bosnia-Herzegovina will be hoping to end their group stage on a high note after nailing down a spot in the League A/B promotion playoffs.

The Dragons were downed 3-2 by group winners Sweden on Saturday, conceding three first-half goals before falling agonisingly short of a comeback with two strikes of their own in the second period.

In fairness to Barbarez's side, that loss was their first of this Nations League campaign following two draws and two wins, including a 4-2 triumph over Tuesday's opponents on September 28.

Heading into this clash, Bosnia-Herzegovina are second with eight points - five behind Sweden but four clear of third-placed Poland - and securing the runners-up spot has presented the Dragons with a shot at ascension to League A.

Another victory in midweek could give the team a boost ahead of their playoff, and fans will be expecting a positive result, given that Barbarez's men have not suffered back-to-back defeats since November 2024.

Meanwhile, Gheorghe Hagi's Romania have delivered a dire campaign so far, but escaping with all three points on Saturday has given them a glimmer of hope.

The Tricolorii lost each of their first four Nations League fixtures this term, conceding 13 goals while scoring just three in the process, and seemed doomed to the League B/C relegation playoffs.

However, a shock 2-1 victory over Poland last time out has placed Group B4's bottom side just one point behind the third-placed Eagles.

Due to their 6-0 thrashing by Poland on October 2, Romania must beat Bosnia-Herzegovina while hoping that their rivals drop points to Sweden in order to secure their future in League B.

That being said, the Tricolorii have not come out on top in any of their eight away matches since hammering San Marino 5-1 in March 2025, losing six times and drawing twice.

Bosnia-Herzegovina have doubts about the readiness of striker Haris Tabakovic, who was forced off just 39 minutes into the clash against Sweden due to a knee injury.

If the Red Bull Salzburg man is unavailable, then Ermedin Demirovic could be joined by Ermin Mahmic up front on Tuesday, supported from out wide by Esmir Bajraktarevic and Kerim Alajbegovic.

At the opposite end of the pitch, centre-back Dennis Hadzikadunic is sidelined with a muscle injury, so Nikola Katic and Stjepan Radeljic should start at the heart of Barbarez's defence.

As for Romania, they are missing midfielder Tudor Baluta, who is suspended for accumulating yellow cards, so Alexandru Cicaldau, Vladimir Screciu and Vlad Dragomir are likely to operate in the centre of the park.

Elsewhere, Florinel Coman and Dennis Man look set to lead the line once again on Tuesday, aided in attack by Alanyaspor's Ianis Hagi.

Bosnia-Herzegovina possible starting lineup:

Zlomislic; Dedic, Katic, Radeljic, Kolasinac; Bajraktarevic, Basic, Gigovic, Alajbegovic; Mahmic, Demirovic

Hindrich; Ratiu, Coubis, Dragusin, Eissat; Cicaldau, Screciu, Dragomir; Hagi; Coman, Man

Bosnia-Herzegovina may have lost to Sweden at the weekend, but they have proven resilient across this Nations League campaign and will be seen as overwhelming favourites on Tuesday.

Romania have struggled in League B, and given their dire away form - not to mention their four defeats this term - it would be surprising to see the visitors avoid another loss.

#1959. Chile vs Colombia - prediction, team news, lineups

By Sam Varley | 16 Nov 2026 04:16

Fresh off the first of two consecutive meetings on Saturday, Chile and Colombia will meet for another international friendly and their final games of 2026 on Tuesday in Santiago.

Tuesday's hosts won the reverse fixture 1-0 away from home, extending their unbeaten streak against Chile.

Chile return to action for their final game of the year on Tuesday aiming to bow out on a positive note after a tough year.

La Roja faced no competitive action in 2026, having fallen short in South American World Cup qualifying last year, meaning they have played just eight times prior to Tuesday's upcoming fixture, losing five and winning three of those.

Nicolas Cordova's team did end the September and October international break with a 2-0 victory over Mexico, thanks to goals from Maximiliano Gutierrez and Vicente Pizarro, but they failed to carry that into the final break of the term, falling short against Colombia again away from home last Saturday.

A trip to Cali ended in a 1-0 loss for La Roja, their fifth defeat in seven games while failing to score for a second time and making it a sixth game against Colombia without a win since a 2019 Copa America penalty shootout triumph.

Now taking their turn to have home advantage for the reverse fixture in Santiago, Chile will set out to end the year with a victory before looking forward and aiming to build in the new year.

Their visitors, meanwhile, make the trip to Santiago aiming to round off their positive year with a double over Chile.

Colombia's 2026 will be remembered for a creditable showing at the World Cup in USA, Mexico and Canada, as La Tricolor topped their group on seven points with two wins and a draw against Portugal.

They would then get past Ghana thanks to Jhon Arias's goal, before falling just short at the hands of Switzerland in the round of 16, losing a penalty shootout after a goalless draw.

In four friendlies since, Nestor Lorenzo's team have won twice, firstly ending the September and October break by beating Peru 2-0 before they beat Chile in Cali on Saturday with a first-half own goal from Guillermo Maripan making the difference.

Now on seven wins in 13 games in the calendar year, Colombia head to Chile looking to make it a perfect final break of 2026 and record another victory.

Nicolas Cordova has a relatively inexperienced Chile squad for the November friendlies, with defenders Paulo Diaz and Benjamin Kuscevic and Paulo Diaz missing out while key midfielder Marcelino Nunez is also not involved.

Ben Brereton Diaz boasts the most experience in a young attacking unit, with 46 caps and 10 international goals to his name, and he may come in from the outset after a substitute appearance in the last game.

That is after Gutierrez, Gonzalo Tapia and Crystal Palace prospect Dario Osorio started in a front three in Colombia, while Rodrigo Echeverria, one of just four players aged above 30 years old, should continue in midfield alongside Vicente Pizarro.

Colombia have also seen plenty of change in their squad, particularly since the World Cup, with James Rodriguez, Juan Quintero and David Ospina retiring while Juan Cuadrado, Santiago Arias, Yerry Mina, Richard Rios and Jhon Duran are also not involved.

Arguably the most notable omission is injured Bayern Munich winger Luis Diaz, leaving La Tricolor light and inexperienced up top.

The line should again be led by Luis Suarez, who has eight goals in 21 caps and 13 in 15 appearances across the Primeira Liga and Champions League for Sporting Lisbon, while a new look squad is headlined by the likes of Daniel Munoz, Davinson Sanchez and Jefferson Lerma.

Vigouroux; Villagra, Maripan, Ulloa; Loyola, Echeverria, Pizarro, Suazo; Osorio, Brereton Diaz, Gutierrez

Vargas; Munoz, Sanchez, Lucumi, Velasquez; Duran, Puerta, Lerma, Perea; Suarez, Arias

Given both sides' relatively limited options at the top end of the pitch, we anticipate another low-scoring encounter on Tuesday and give the edge to the visitors to complete a double over Chile.

#1957. How Michael Carrick's Man United fell apart: Players' bust-up on flight back from Madrid, weakness in training and on touchline - and why dressing-room sources believe divided board 'hung him out to dry'

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER and NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER

Published: 10:30 EST, 11 November 2026 | Updated: 06:44 EST, 12 November 2026

For the last two days, Michael Carrick has followed his familiar route towards Manchester United’s training base, nudging his black Land Rover past the security barrier at Carrington before 8am, and making his way into work just as he has for much of the last two decades as a player, coach and head coach at the club.

While Carrick's fate has been decided by men in suits in Monaco and Manchester, he has put on his training gear and gone through the motions of coaching whichever players are left during the international break.

It has become increasingly apparent that Carrick was a dead man walking in the two weeks since the United board gave him a stay of execution and bought themselves time after the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth last month.

Having effectively been brought in as a caretaker when United plucked him off the beach in Barbados in mid-January, he left much the same way: merely keeping the seat warm for Mauricio Pochettino in the chaotic days that have led to his sacking.

Sources close to the United dressing room believe Carrick has been ‘hung out to dry’ as United dithered over his future and then began a futile attempt to appoint Pochettino as his replacement in secret.

This is the story of how Carrick's United fell apart. It is the story of how disgruntled players aired their dirty laundry in public and clashed in private. It is the story of how the club's boardroom became the backdrop for an executive power struggle. And it is the story of how the magic touch that saw Carrick land the job permanently just five months ago deserted him...

Michael Carrick is out as Manchester United manager - just ten league games after guiding United to third and being handed a two-year contract

Carrick has had to turn up as normal at Carrington this week even as the world knew he was for the chop. Some dressing-room sources say he has been 'hung out to dry'

Carrick would have seen the writing on the wall when he got up to give an impressive speech at a dinner in the Heritage Suite at Old Trafford on Friday night to celebrate the 40th anniversary of Sir Alex Ferguson’s appointment.

The significance of the occasion was not lost on Carrick. Ferguson was brought in to succeed Ron Atkinson on the same date in November 1986 with United one place above the relegation zone. Having boxed himself into an identical corner, Carrick too was on borrowed time.

Two days later, he stood helplessly on the touchline at Old Trafford as United played out a ridiculous 4-4 draw with Aston Villa. Twice his team fought back from two goals down, but it was the final proof for United bosses that change was unavoidable.

The biggest club in English football having to endure the humiliation of at least two weeks in the relegation zone was too much for them to stomach.

His body language after the Bournemouth game when a tearful and crestfallen Carrick offered what looked like a farewell wave to the Stretford End – four days after he approached fans in Como to apologise for an equally painful 4-1 Champions League surrender – suggested he was already done.

The 45-year-old limped on to another defeat at Chelsea, then presided over a barmy 3-2 comeback win over Roma and the bonkers draw with Villa. A consummate and composed midfielder for United, Carrick of all people knew this wasn’t the way football should be played.

All the while, he spoke like a man who could turn things around. They always do. But the performances and results told a different story.

His critics would argue that someone whose only previous job in management was at Middlesbrough should never have been put in charge of United in the first place.

Others would say the bravest move by the club would have been to thank Carrick for his admirable efforts in securing third place and Champions League qualification last season, and move on in the summer when Pochettino would have been available for free before signing a new contract as US coach with a £7million release clause.

Matheus Cunha's late winner sealed a remarkable comeback win over Roma last week - but it promised to be a false dawn for Carrick

The 45-year-old's body language after an earlier loss to Bournemouth had suggested he was done back then, with Carrick appearing to wave farewell to the Stretford End

Instead, Carrick was rewarded with a two-year deal in May and the wheels fell off in spectacular fashion. Rather like his friend and former team-mate Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, the honeymoon period gave way to something altogether less appealing.

At least Solskjaer stuck around for three more years. Having beaten the Norwegian to the job in January, Carrick’s reign lasted less than 10 months.

The similarities between the two men are striking. Ex-players who basked in the glory days under Ferguson and know what it takes to succeed at Old Trafford, but were incapable of lifting the modern-day Manchester United to similar heights.

Having replaced Ruben Amorim and inspired a remarkable turnaround in the second half of last season, Carrick must have thought he had a chance.

His calm demeanour and experience of life in the Old Trafford pressure cooker that had played a part in his appointment was in contrast to the emotional incontinence of Amorim. How strange then that it has given way to such calamity and chaos.

United got off to the worst possible start by losing at newly-promoted Hull City in August. Tigers boss Sergej Jakirovic belittled them by saying his goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis might as well have been sipping a cup of tea, and the hits have just kept on coming for Carrick.

Aside from Bournemouth, there were the late equalisers scored by Ainsley Maitland-Niles and Dominic Solanke for Everton and Tottenham, the controversial winner conceded to 10-man Manchester City, crashing out of the Carabao Cup to Brighton after giving up a two-goal lead, and the defeats in Europe by Atletico Madrid and Como after going behind in the opening seconds.

By the time Alysson scored in the first minute for Villa on Sunday, United’s defence had become as leaky as the Old Trafford roof. The four goals Carrick’s side conceded took it to 15 in his final four games.

United's defence has been leaky all season long, with Ainsley Maitland-Niles' stoppage-time equaliser at Hill Dickinson Stadium among the goals to cost them valuable points

By the time Alysson scored in the first minute for Aston Villa on Sunday, United’s defence had become as leaky as the Old Trafford roof. They let in 15 in his final four games

So why the alarming decline from last season? The United players haven’t looked sharp after a disjointed World Cup summer that involved a more relaxed one-week training camp in Ireland. There have been too many injuries.

Some players have spoken of a drop-off in training under Carrick and his backroom staff. Others feel that the switch to a more possession-based 4-2-4 system was asking too much of a group who aren’t suited to it.

There was surprise that a man so invested in the club's academy used so few young players. Harry Amass was left kicking his heels despite the chronic shortage of left backs, JJ Gabriel's shock exit was an unwelcome distraction, and Shea Lacey's re-emergence came too late.

It would be grossly unfair to pin this all on Carrick though. He is just the latest unfortunate to pay the price for the shambles at United which runs from the boardroom to the dressing room.

Amid ongoing uncertainty over his future, there has been a power struggle behind the scenes between director of football Jason Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell over who to replace him, while sources close to the Glazer family have revealed a growing dissatisfaction at how minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos are running the club.

United failed Carrick in the transfer market last summer with a futile pursuit of his No 1 midfield target Elliot Anderson, and instead delivered Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos.

Carrick could see trouble on the horizon when he spoke to the media at Carton House in Maynooth during that pre-season camp in early August, but tried not to rock the boat.

It was the day his daughter Louise was getting her A-level results. ‘You know, we would like more, we need to keep pushing for more,’ he said, using the word ‘push’ another nine times.

There has been a power struggle behind the scenes between director of football Jason Wilcox (centre) and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell (left) over who to replace Carrick

Some players have spoken of a drop-off in training under Carrick and his backroom staff

Carlos Baleba followed but an ankle injury meant that he couldn’t play until October, and the £70m signing then suffered a hamstring injury.

United blundered catastrophically by focusing on midfield and delaying improvements to other areas of the team until next summer. In particular, the decision not to sign cover for Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko backfired spectacularly as both players succumbed to injury.

Lisandro Martinez called out United’s underwhelming recruitment in Madrid by saying he expected more of Wilcox, and he isn’t the only one who feels that way.

Tielemans gave a terse ‘no comment’ when he was asked on camera about his team-mate’s remarks, but it’s understood the two players clashed on the team flight back to Manchester as cracks began to show in an increasingly unhappy camp.

The camaraderie fostered by rounds of golf involving Carrick and the players during the break in Ireland was beginning to fall apart.

It came to a head when captain Bruno Fernandes became the second member of the leadership group to speak out of turn, questioning Carrick’s tactics after the loss to Como.

Having continuously defended his players in the face of criticism from some of his former United team-mates over their lack of effort, Carrick’s spiky response that ‘if you don't run forward and you don't run back, you aren’t going to win’ perhaps revealed his true feelings about this group.

He and Fernandes settled their differences in a clear-the-air meeting, but the questions didn’t go away. When he was asked about their relationship again at the end of what proved to be his final pre-match press conference last Friday, Carrick tapped his inquisitor on the shoulder as he left the room at Carrington and said with a smile: ‘Nice try!’

It was typical of Carrick, who often met questions with the knowing grin of a man who couldn’t say what he really thought.

Lisandro Martinez and Youri Tielemans clashed on United's flight back to Manchester following the former's incendiary comments after a loss to Atletico Madrid

One issue has been Carrick’s rather passionless appearance on the touchline. ‘He doesn't upset anyone, but doesn't inspire anyone either,’ remarked one dressing room source

It got to the point where he was encouraged by the club to be a little more forthcoming in press conferences. There have been some barbed post-match exchanges in TV interviews with Sky Sports and Viaplay this season, and the five-minute monologue before the Bournemouth game was pure theatre.

But on the whole, Carrick’s ability to play a straight bat in front of the cameras was a welcome change for the Old Trafford hierarchy compared to the loose-lipped Amorim – particularly with the Amazon Prime documentary-makers following their every move.

‘He talks a lot but doesn't say much,’ said Roy Keane, never Carrick’s biggest fan, on Sunday. ‘I don't know if that's a tactic, like a politician.’

More of an issue was Carrick’s rather passionless appearance on the touchline, which seemed to be reflected in his team at times.

Always dressed in black, a hand placed studiously on his chin, it has contrasted with more animated adversaries such as Unai Emery, Roberto De Zerbi and Diego Simeone in recent weeks.

‘He doesn't upset anyone, but doesn't inspire anyone either,’ remarked one dressing room source.

The fans were always behind him though, even the ones who may have accepted some time ago that a change was needed. Support and sympathy were never in short supply for a coach who has been let down by the men in the directors’ box and the players on the pitch.

That much has been abundantly clear by the abuse meted out to Ratcliffe and Co this season, and the unprecedented scenes when the fans turned on the players after Bournemouth.

Carrick looks set to be replaced by former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Mauricio Pochettino (right)

Carrick has been known to stand alongside them in the past, and it would be no surprise to see him there again in future.

‘Oh, it’s Carrick you know…’ echoed his tribute song from the Stretford End as he disappeared down the tunnel for the last time on Sunday evening.

So another bites the dust. A good man. A United man. The right man for the job? Maybe not, as it turns out. That poisoned chalice now passes to Mauricio Pochettino.

#1956. Cardinale says pre-season is ‘up to Amorim’ as Milan will not chase ‘extra two million’

Gerry Cardinale has provided some refreshing comments on Milan’s pre-season plans for the future, confirming that money will no longer dictate where they go.

Over the last ten years or so, it has become far more common for big clubs to travel across the world for their pre-season campaigns. For example, Milan have been in Australia for two consecutive pre-seasons now, taking on Perth Glory and most recently Inter.

While it’s great to connect with local fan bases, the travel is demanding for the players. This summer, Milan played games in Glasgow (Scotland), Perth (Australia), Jakarta (Indonesia), and Wroclaw (Poland). resulting in a lot of travel.

Speaking about the pre-season in his long interview with Gazzetta dello Sport, Cardinale said that the upcoming pre-season planning will be decided by Ruben Amorim. Money will no longer dictate where they go. Instead, the best plan for preparing the players will be chosen.

In an effort to generate new revenue, are you also considering a tour for AC Milan next summer? Will that still be Australia or the United States?

“We have already discussed it with Amorim, and I will just tell you that if we play friendlies abroad, they will be in the United States next summer. If we do… We haven’t decided yet, and the decision will be up to Ruben.

“It will depend on what’s best for the team: playing friendlies abroad must add value to the group, not bring in a couple of million for the club. Those extra two million will no longer be our goal, as they were under the previous management. That won’t happen again under this ownership.

“Everything we organise in terms of friendlies will be carefully considered with our coach. Every move. And we won’t participate in tours organised by others. We put our players first. We want to help them prepare well to win. That’s our goal, and we aim to achieve it as soon as possible.”

#1954. Joe Hart: Liverpool must have ‘grown-up conversations’ over dilemma with ‘adopted Scouser’

Joe Hart has said that Liverpool need to have ‘grown-up conversations’ with Alisson Becker regarding his contract situation at Anfield.

The Reds’ long-serving number 1 – who turned 34 in October – has just over seven months remaining on his existing deal, and he recently expressed his desire to remain on Merseyside beyond next summer.

The Brazilian’s agent Ze Maria has indicated that ‘preliminary talks’ are underway with LFC rearding a possible extension for the goalkeeper, who produced an outstanding performance in the win at Crystal Palace prior to the international break.

Speaking on The Overlap Fan Debate, Hart believes that Alisson will be offered a new contract, but the length of those terms could pose a tricky dilemma for the relevant parties.

The ex-England goalkeeper said: “In his eyes there’s still a lot of legs in him, so you’ve gotta be really careful. I imagine Liverpool will offer him a new contract, but they can’t offer him a one-year contract. Can they offer him two (years) with everything that’s gone on, and then you talk about balancing wages?

“I think there needs to be some grown-up conversations behind the scenes. Are Liverpool capable of having those conversations with Alisson? He’s the kind of guy who wants Liverpool to do well.

“He’s an adopted Scouser and I love that about him. He’s one of the best to play in the Premier League, but are Liverpool capable of having those grown-up conversations with him? It felt a bit fractious with him towards the end of last season and potentially he was looking elsewhere.”

Under FSG, Liverpool rarely offer lucrative contract extensions to players over the age of 30, although they made a notable exception for Mo Salah in April 2025, and such is Alisson’s legacy and importance that he too could be afforded special treatment.

He’s currently on £250,000 per week, a figure exceeded by just six of his teammates (Capology), so any renewal would either see the club commit to a significant financial outlay, or the goalkeeper accepting lower wages to remain at Anfield for at least one more year.

Hart’s point about the length of any new contract offer is pertinent. Do Liverpool offer just 12 months and find themselves back at this juncture again next autumn? Do they agree to pay him a high salary for two more seasons, at the end of which he’d be nearly 37?

The Reds have Giorgi Mamardashvili and (from next summer) Lucca Brughmans as prospective long-term successors to Alisson, but such is the world-class brilliance of our number 1 that keeping him for as long as possible seems a no-brainer.

Imagine what the incoming Belgian teenager could learn from the Brazil veteran if the latter is still around to impart priceless advice gleaned from years of playing at an elite level.

Fingers crossed that all parties can find a mutually satisfactory agreement which’ll keep our number 1 at Anfield until at least the summer of 2028.

#1952. Mauritania vs Burkina Faso - prediction, team news, lineups

By Joshua Ojele | 16 Nov 2026 06:06, Last updated: 16 Nov 2026 06:12

Mauritania and Burkina Faso are back in action in the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifiers when they go head to head at the Stade Cheikha Ould Boidiya on Tuesday evening.

With just four points between first and third in the Group F standings midway through the qualifiers, both nations know the result here could prove decisive in shaping their qualification ambitions.

Having kicked off their Africa Cup of Nations qualifying journey with much promise, consecutive defeats in their last two outings have seen Mauritania's fortunes take a turn for the worse.

Aboubakary Koita, Mamadou Diallo and Alverca striker Dawda Camara all hit the target to fire Les Mourabitounes to a 3-1 opening-day victory over Central African Republic on September 24, five days before crashing back to earth in a 2-1 loss against Benin.

Aritz Lopez Garai’s side were left red-faced on their return to the qualifiers at the weekend, when they fell to a 1-0 defeat against Burkina Faso in the first of their November double-header at the Stade du 4 Aout, with Moise Kabore netting the winner in the 91st minute to sink the visitors.

Having missed the 2025 AFCON, Mauritania find themselves under pressure for a result heading into Tuesday as they sit third in the Group F standings, behind Benin and Burkina Faso, who sit tied on seven points in the first two places.

As for Burkina Faso, head coach Amir Abdou will be pleased with his side’s display on Friday, particularly as it represents a positive response to their crushing 7-0 friendly defeat at the hands of three-time World Champions Argentina in their previous outing on October 4.

The Stallions are now closing on a third straight competitive victory since October 2024, after kicking off their AFCON qualifying campaign with a 1-1 stalemate against Benin in Ouagadougou on September 25, three days before securing a 1-0 win over Central African Republic thanks to a 60th-minute strike from Salzburg striker Aboubacar Camara.

Burkina Faso, who sit 62nd in the latest FIFA World Rankings, are aiming to secure a fourth consecutive AFCON appearance, having finished fourth in 2021 before consecutive round-of-16 exits in 2023 and 2025 respectively.

Abdou’s men will be backing themselves to take pole position in Group F on Tuesday when they take on an opposing side who have failed to win 10 of the previous 12 meetings between the two nations, losing seven and claiming three draws since May 1987.

Burkina Faso Africa Cup of Nations Qualifying form:

JS Kabylie defender Aly Abeid was forced off injured midway through the game against Burkina Faso at the weekend, and the 28-year-old is a doubt for Tuesday's tie.

In his absence, Olympique Akbou full-back Khadim Diaw should come into the fold, forming the back four with Ibrahima Keita, Mohamed Ali Diadie and Angers’ man Jordan Lefort.

At the attacking end of the pitch, we expect to see an unchanged front three of Abdoullah Ba, Djeidi Gassama and 26-year-old striker Ndiaga Yade, with ZED FC midfielder Maata Magassa retaining his role at the centre of the park.

Off the back of another solid defensive display, we expect Burkina Faso to name an unchanged back four on Tuesday, with Mamoutou Ouedraogo, Nasser Djiga, Edmond Tapsoba and Arsene Kouassi shielding skipper Herve Koffi between the sticks.

Kabore turned in an eye-catching display to hand the Stallions all three points against Mauritania last time out, and the teenage striker could be rewarded with a starting role here, with Lassina Traore, who has failed to find the back of the net in nine games for club and country since September, swearing over his role in the XI.

While Mauritania have shown flashes of brilliance in the qualifiers, they find themselves on the cusp of a damaging third consecutive defeat and will be keen to rise to the occasion on Tuesday.

However, Burkina Faso boast superior quality and experience in their rank — particularly at the defensive end of the pitch — and we expect the difference in individual quality to be a decisive factor here, with the Stallions claiming another narrow victory.

#1946. Man City: Why the international break could be vital for Maresca

By Axel Clody | 16 Nov 2026 06:59

Manchester City began the season with the impression that adapting to Enzo Maresca’s work would be quick. With seven wins in the opening Premier League rounds, the team took the lead and at one point opened up a six-point advantage over Arsenal. The run, however, was abruptly interrupted.

Defeats to Aston Villa, Brighton and Nottingham Forest dropped the team to third place and allowed the current champions to pull clear at the top.

More than the scorelines, the performances exposed difficulties in competing physically, winning duels and protecting the defence when possession is lost. Maresca himself acknowledged that his team could not keep up with the intensity of the opposition in the first half.

So the November international break comes at a good time. The pause will not erase the problems that have appeared in recent weeks, nor does it mean that all the players will have days off. But it offers the manager a valuable opportunity to assess performance, recover players and work on adjustments that would hardly be possible with a run of matches.

The drop in City’s level cannot be explained only by a lack of efficiency in front of goal.

The team can still control possession and produce offensive volume. Against Forest, for example, it finished the game with 79 per cent possession and 12 shots. The problem is that this control has not been enough to stop opponents finding space and creating dangerous situations.

One of the main issues is defensive protection. City have conceded 17 goals in eight matches and have not kept a clean sheet in any of their last nine games. The high defensive line, a hallmark of Maresca’s teams, demands coordination between the units and a quick ability to react to losing the ball. When the counter-press does not work, the defenders are left exposed to fast attacks and have to defend large spaces.

The absence of Rodri helps to explain part of this difficulty. The Spaniard offered reading of the game, interceptions and the quality to organise the build-up. More than a defensive midfielder who protects the defence, he is a player capable of anticipating danger and stopping counter-attacks before they gather speed. Without him, the rest of the midfield has to share responsibilities that Rodri used to take on almost alone.

Elliot Anderson has been important in this context, but so too is the distribution of roles. The presence of players such as Enzo Fernandez and Rayan Cherki adds technical quality and creativity, but also demands defensive cover. If the two play together without a structure that protects the central area, Anderson can be overburdened in covering and in physical duels.

The break allows Maresca to work on these relationships. One possibility is to adjust the make-up of the midfield, ensuring more balance between creation and protection. Another is to review the team’s positioning without the ball, especially the distance between the defensive line and the most advanced players. It is not necessarily a question of abandoning the style of play, but of finding ways to make it less vulnerable.

The calendar and the physical condition of the squad are another important aspect. City lost rhythm during a demanding period of fixtures, and the recovery of players can help the team regain the intensity needed to execute Maresca’s model.

It will also be important to monitor the situation of Marc Guehi and Josko Gvardiol. Both were substituted at half-time against Nottingham Forest because of physical problems, according to Maresca. The break could be useful to assess the extent of the issues and avoid important players returning before they are fully fit.

There is, however, a caveat: the international break is not a holiday for the whole squad. Several starters have been called up by their national teams, among them Erling Haaland, Gianluigi Donnarumma, Ruben Dias, Gvardiol, Guehi, Enzo Fernandez and Cherki. Travel and international commitments reduce the recovery time for some players, while others will be able to stay in Manchester and work directly with the coaching staff.

Even so, the break offers an opportunity to reorganise the workload and prepare the squad for what follows. In a season in which intensity is essential to the functioning of Maresca’s system, managing physical wear and tear is also part of the recovery process.

The break arrives at a time when City need to recover not only results, but also confidence in their own way of playing. The seven opening wins showed that the team has the resources to compete for the title. The three defeats that followed, on the other hand, revealed that there are still important adjustments to be made to sustain that level over an entire season.

The first challenge after the break will be against Fulham at the Etihad Stadium. Then the team will face an even more significant fixture: the visit to Arsenal on 29 November. The six-point gap makes the direct meeting an important opportunity to close the distance, although the result will not be enough, by itself, to settle the title race.

For Maresca, the international break is a chance to find answers before the run of negative results turns into an even bigger problem. The manager needs to restore defensive solidity, find the best distribution of roles in midfield and make possession dominance translate into effective control of matches again.

City do not need to abandon their identity to react. Above all, they need to find a better balance between what they do with the ball and what they can do when they lose it. If the break allows Maresca to progress with this work and recover important players, the team could return better prepared to face a decisive stretch of the season.
